MODULES.title: LLM Fundamentals
MODULES.tag: Tokens, context, sampling, model families: the vocabulary layer
MODULES.why: Every AI system you'll oversee sits on top of an LLM API. If you aren't fluent in tokens, context windows, sampling, and model families, you can't make a sound call on cost, latency, or quality.
MODULES.mental: An LLM is a function call to a stateless, slow, expensive, probabilistic, context-bounded text-completion service. Every architectural decision flows from those five adjectives. Stateless means you pass the history yourself. Slow means latency budgets and streaming. Expensive means cost discipline. Probabilistic means evals and guardrails. Context-bounded means retrieval and compression.
concepts: Token
The unit an LLM processes, roughly ¾ of an English word (~4 chars). Pricing, context limits, and latency are all measured in tokens. Fewer per word for code and non-Latin scripts.
Context window

Max tokens (input + output) per call. 1M windows are now standard across hosted frontier models (verified Aug 9, 2026). But filling 1M tokens costs real money — $0.14–$10 per call depending on model, a ~70× spread — and long context still degrades, 'lost in the middle' didn't disappear.
Input vs output tokens
Priced separately; output is typically 3–5× more expensive and is where latency comes from (generated one token at a time).
Sampling
temperature (randomness), top_p (nucleus), max_tokens, stop sequences. Use temperature OR top_p aggressively, not both. T=0 reduces randomness but is NOT deterministic across calls.
Model families — the shape that lasts

Every provider ships the same shape: a flagship for the hard 5%, a workhorse mid-tier, and a cheap/fast tier for triage — plus an open-weight ecosystem underneath. Reasoning modes burn extra internal tokens for harder tasks. Magnitudes that matter (verified Aug 9, 2026): output runs ~3–5× input price; cheap-to-flagship spans ~10× within a lineup and ~70× across the market. Current names, prices and the who's-who live in the 2026 Model Landscape module — one source, refreshed quarterly.
Latency anatomy
TTFT (time to first token) + TPS × output length. Streaming hides TTFT, not total time.
Prompt caching
Cache the static prefix (system prompt, retrieved docs). Cuts input cost up to 90% on repeated context. The single biggest cost lever after model choice.
Batch API
~50% discount for async work that can wait. Ideal for nightly evals and bulk classification.
mistakes: Treating temperature=0 as deterministic, providers don't guarantee bitwise reproducibility
Underestimating output token cost, output dominates the bill
Using premium models for trivial routing/classification
No fallback when the provider has an outage
Not accounting for tokenizer differences across providers when porting prompts, the same text can cost 15–30% more tokens on a different model family
Assuming a 1M window means you should fill it, cost and quality both degrade
flags: "We're using the flagship model for everything", nobody right-sized
"We don't track token usage per feature", no cost discipline
"We just call the SDK directly", no gateway → no fallback, caching, observability, or model swap
"We don't version our prompts", every change is a silent prod incident
ask: What's our cost per request, broken into input/output tokens?
Why this model and not the next tier down?
What happens when the provider rate-limits or 5xx's?
What % of our prompt tokens hit the cache?

MODULES.title: Prompt Engineering
MODULES.tag: The cheapest, fastest quality lever you own
MODULES.why: Prompt changes are free, instant, and routinely worth 10–30 points of task accuracy. Pull this lever first, before you fine-tune, switch models, or add complexity.
MODULES.mental: A prompt is a program written in natural language, executed by a probabilistic interpreter. Like any program, it needs structure, examples, explicit output contracts, and version control. Unlike any program, it fails silently and gradually, so it needs regression tests (evals).
concepts: System vs user messages
System prompt sets persistent behavior, constraints, and persona; user messages carry the task. Models weight system instructions heavily, put non-negotiables there.
Few-shot examples
2–5 input→output examples beat paragraphs of instruction. Examples define format, tone, and edge-case handling implicitly.
Chain of thought
'Think step by step' or structured reasoning fields measurably improve hard-task accuracy. Native reasoning models internalize this, don't double-prompt them to reason.
Structured output
JSON schema / function-calling-enforced output. Eliminates parsing failures. Always prefer schema enforcement over 'please respond in JSON'.
XML/markdown sectioning
Delimit context, instructions, examples, and data with clear tags. Models parse structure far more reliably than prose blobs.
Prompt versioning
Prompts are code: version-controlled, code-reviewed, eval-gated before deploy. A prompt change without an eval run is a blind deploy.
Negative instructions
Models follow 'do X' far better than 'don't do Y'. Reframe prohibitions as positive instructions with examples.
mistakes: Iterating on vibes, changing prompts without an eval set is guessing
One mega-prompt doing five jobs, decompose into focused calls
Stuffing instructions in the user turn that belong in system
Begging for JSON instead of enforcing schema
Prompting reasoning models with elaborate CoT scaffolding they no longer need
flags: "The prompt is in the codebase somewhere", unversioned, untested
"We tweaked the prompt and shipped it Friday", no regression gate
"Our prompt is 6,000 tokens", likely doing too many jobs, blowing cache efficiency
ask: Where does this prompt live, and what gates a change to it?
What eval set runs before a prompt change deploys?
Which parts of the prompt are static (cacheable) vs dynamic?

MODULES.title: Context Engineering
MODULES.tag: Curating what the model sees: the discipline that ate prompt engineering
MODULES.why: The 2025–26 consensus is that managing WHAT goes into the window matters more than wordsmithing instructions. Agents, RAG, memory, and harnesses are all context engineering problems. Prompt engineering isn't irrelevant; clear instructions still matter. But in agentic systems, what the model sees outweighs how it's phrased. Prompt engineering designs the instructions. Context engineering decides what else is in the room when the model reads them.
MODULES.mental: Treat the context window as RAM, and yourself as the operating system. You decide what gets loaded, what gets paged out, what gets compressed, and what gets fetched on demand. The model only knows what's in RAM right now.
concepts: Context budget
Allocate the window deliberately: system prompt + tools + retrieved docs + history + scratchpad + output reserve. Track utilization like a memory profiler.
Lost in the middle
Models attend best to the start and end of context. Put critical instructions at the start, the immediate question at the end; don't bury key facts mid-window.
Compaction / summarization

When history exceeds budget, summarize older turns into a compact state. This is how agent harnesses (e.g. Claude Code) run long sessions; compaction is lossy, critical state must live in files or structured notes, not only in the summary.
Just-in-time retrieval
Don't preload everything, give the model tools to fetch what it needs (file reads, search) when it needs it. Agentic search often beats one-shot RAG stuffing.
Context rot
Quality degrades as windows fill with stale tool output, dead ends, and repetition. Prune aggressively; a clean 30K context beats a noisy 200K one.
Cache-aware layout
Order context stable→volatile: system prompt and tool defs first (cached), per-request data last. Reordering breaks the cache prefix.
Sub-agent isolation
Spin off a fresh-context sub-agent for a noisy subtask (e.g. broad search), return only the conclusion. Keeps the main context clean.
mistakes: Stuffing the window because it fits, cost and accuracy both suffer
Letting raw tool output accumulate unpruned
Putting volatile data before stable data (kills prompt caching)
Relying on compaction alone for critical state, write it to durable artifacts
Preloading 50 documents when the agent could fetch the 2 it needs
flags: "Our average request uses 150K context", almost certainly unpruned noise
"We lose track of what the agent did earlier in long sessions", no compaction strategy, no progress files
"Cache hit rate is near zero", context layout is volatile-first
ask: What's our context budget breakdown for a typical request?
How do we handle conversations that outgrow the window?
What's our prompt cache hit rate, and what breaks it?

MODULES.title: 2026 Model Landscape
MODULES.tag: Who's who as of Aug 9, 2026, and how to choose
MODULES.why: Model choice is the highest-impact cost and quality decision on any AI project. The lineup shifts quarterly. The decision framework doesn't.
MODULES.mental: Models are interchangeable commodities behind a gateway; your moat is the harness, evals, and data. Pick per-task tiers, re-benchmark quarterly on YOUR evals (not leaderboards), and keep switching cost near zero.
concepts: Current flagships (verified Aug 9, 2026)

Claude Fable 5 tops Anthropic's lineup; Claude Opus 5 (July 24) is the drop-in workhorse successor to Opus 4.8. GPT-5.6 GA'd July 9 (Luna/Terra/Sol — Sol is the flagship). Gemini 3.6 Flash (July 21) is Google's newest, with Gemini 4 teased but unreleased. Grok 4.5 (July 8): 500K context, native video input.
Pricing reality

Fable 5: $10/$50 per M tokens; Opus 5 (and Opus 4.8): $5/$25. GPT-5.6 Sol: $5/$30; Luna: $0.20/$1.20 after the July 30 cut. Gemini 3.6 Flash: $1.50/$7.50; Haiku 4.5 ($1/$5) anchors the budget tier. Sonnet 5's $2/$10 intro pricing ends Aug 31 ($3/$15 after). Filling the same 1M window: $0.14 (DeepSeek V4 Flash) to $10 (Fable 5), a 71× spread — verified Aug 9, 2026.
1M+ context is table stakes
13+ hosted frontier models ship ≥1M windows. The differentiator is no longer window size, it's effective recall across the window, cost to fill it, and latency.
Reasoning as a dial, not a model
Most flagships now expose adjustable thinking/reasoning effort rather than separate reasoning SKUs. Spend reasoning tokens on hard tasks only.
Open weights are frontier-adjacent

DeepSeek V4, Qwen 3.6, MiniMax M3, and GLM-5 are credible for high-volume, cost-sensitive, or data-residency-bound workloads, if you can fund the MLOps. Llama 4 is still the most-deployed family, but it's legacy-scale now, not frontier.
Tiering strategy
Cheap/fast tier (Haiku, Flash, mini) for triage, classification, extraction; mid tier for the workhorse; flagship/reasoning for the hardest 5% of calls. Route, don't default.
Benchmarks lie (a little)
Leaderboard deltas compress in practice, and harness quality swamps model deltas on agentic tasks. Your own eval suite on your own data is the only score that matters.
mistakes: Hard-coding one provider's SDK everywhere, no gateway means no leverage
Chasing every release, re-benchmark quarterly, not weekly
Choosing by leaderboard rather than your own evals
Ignoring open-weight options at scale (10–50× unit cost difference)
Buying the flagship for workloads a small model handles at equal accuracy
flags: "We can't switch models, too much rework", vendor lock-in by architecture
"We picked it because it tops LMArena", nobody validated on real traffic
"All traffic goes to one model", no tiering, no routing
ask: What would it take to swap providers next week?
When did we last re-benchmark our top 3 routes?
What fraction of calls actually need flagship-tier quality?

MODULES.title: RAG Systems & Pipelines
MODULES.tag: The dominant production pattern for grounding models in your data
MODULES.why: RAG is still the best way to make a model answer from YOUR knowledge with citations, freshness, and access control. Fine-tuning and long context alone give you none of those.
MODULES.mental: RAG is a search problem wearing an AI costume. Retrieval quality caps answer quality. If the right passage never gets retrieved, no prompt or model will save you. Get search relevance right first, then worry about generation.
concepts: The pipeline
Ingest → chunk → embed → index → (query) retrieve → rerank → assemble context → generate → cite. Every stage has failure modes; instrument each.
Chunking
Split documents semantically (headings, paragraphs), not at fixed character counts. Typical: 200–800 tokens with overlap or contextual headers. Bad chunking is the #1 silent RAG killer.
Hybrid retrieval
Dense vectors (semantic) + BM25/keyword (exact terms, IDs, names) + metadata filters. Pure vector search misses part numbers, names, and acronyms; hybrid is the production default.
Reranking

A cross-encoder reranks the top 50–100 candidates to surface the best 5–10 for the model's context. Cheap, large quality win, the most under-used stage. In practice, retrieval fetches ~50 candidates, the reranker scores them, and the top 5–10 (depending on your context budget) go to generation.
Query transformation
Rewrite the user's question for retrieval: expansion, decomposition into sub-queries, HyDE. Conversational queries especially need rewriting with history context.
Agentic RAG
The 2026 evolution: the model decides when and what to search, issues multiple queries, evaluates results, and iterates, retrieval as a tool, not a fixed pre-step.
RAG vs long context
Long context handles 'analyze this one document'; RAG handles 'answer from a corpus too large/dynamic/permissioned to send'. They compose: retrieve broadly, then load full docs JIT.
Citations & grounding
Force answers to cite retrieved chunk IDs; reject or flag answers with no supporting chunk. Your main hallucination defense.
mistakes: Evaluating only the final answer, not retrieval (recall@k) separately
Fixed-size chunking that splits tables and sentences mid-thought
Vector-only search, fails on exact identifiers
No reranker, top-k raw vector hits go straight into context
Ignoring document permissions in retrieval (data leak via RAG)
Skipping freshness: stale index serving deleted/edited docs
flags: "Our RAG answers are bad" with no retrieval metrics, they're debugging blind
"We chunk at 500 characters", arbitrary, format-blind
"Everyone searches the same index", permission model missing
ask: What's retrieval recall@10 on our golden set?
How do we know when retrieval, not generation, failed?
How fast does an edited document reach the index?
How are document ACLs enforced at query time?

MODULES.title: Embeddings
MODULES.tag: Meaning as geometry: the substrate under retrieval
MODULES.why: Embeddings power retrieval, dedup, clustering, recommendation, and semantic caching. Choosing them well and running them well is the foundation under every RAG and memory system.
MODULES.mental: An embedding model is a lossy compression of meaning into a point in space, where distance is roughly semantic similarity. Like any lossy codec, it's tuned for a domain, and mixing codecs corrupts the archive. You can never compare vectors from different models.
concepts: What they are
Dense vectors (typically 256–3072 dims) from a dedicated embedding model (not your chat LLM). Similar meaning → nearby vectors (cosine similarity).
Model choice
OpenAI text-embedding-3, Cohere embed-v4, Voyage, open-weight BGE/GTE/E5. Check the MTEB leaderboard but validate on YOUR retrieval task, domain match beats benchmark rank.
Dimensions tradeoff
Bigger = better quality, more storage/latency/cost. Matryoshka embeddings let you truncate dims with graceful degradation, store big, query small.
One model rule
Query and documents MUST use the same embedding model and version. A model upgrade means re-embedding the whole corpus, plan migration like a schema change.
Asymmetric embedding
Queries and documents are different text types; modern models accept input_type hints (query vs document). Use them.
Beyond retrieval
Semantic cache (skip duplicate LLM calls), near-dup detection, clustering for topic discovery, anomaly detection on drift.
Fine-tuned embeddings
For specialized jargon (legal, medical, internal codenames), fine-tuning the embedder lifts recall far more cheaply than fine-tuning the LLM.
mistakes: Comparing vectors from different models/versions, silent garbage results
Embedding entire documents in one vector, chunk first
Forgetting to re-embed after a model upgrade
Cosine similarity on unnormalized vectors when the index expects normalized
Treating 0.8 similarity as universally 'similar', thresholds are model- and domain-specific
flags: "We upgraded the embedding model last sprint" + no re-embedding ticket, the index is corrupted
"Why is similarity weird?", usually mixed models or missing input_type
Storage bill growing linearly with docs at 3072 dims, nobody considered truncation
ask: Which embedding model and version, and where is that pinned?
What's our re-embedding plan for a model upgrade?
Did we evaluate against our domain or just trust MTEB?

MODULES.title: Vector Databases
MODULES.tag: Approximate search at scale, and when you don't need one
MODULES.why: The vector DB you pick locks in cost, latency, scale ceiling, and operational burden for every retrieval-backed feature. Getting it wrong hurts both ways: overkill wastes money, underkill caps you.
MODULES.mental: A vector DB is a search index, not a database of record. It answers 'what's nearby?' fast by being approximately right (ANN). Your source of truth lives elsewhere. The index is rebuildable, disposable infrastructure.
concepts: ANN algorithms
HNSW (graph, fast queries, RAM-heavy), IVF (cluster-based), ScaNN/DiskANN (disk-scale). All trade recall for speed, tune ef_search/nprobe and MEASURE recall.
The landscape

Dedicated: Pinecone, Qdrant, Weaviate, Milvus. Bolt-on: pgvector (Postgres), OpenSearch/Elastic, Redis. Embedded: LanceDB, Chroma, FAISS. Bolt-on wins below ~10M vectors if you already run that infra.
pgvector first
If you run Postgres and have <5–10M vectors, pgvector with HNSW is usually the right answer: one less system, transactions, joins with your relational data, real ACLs.
Metadata filtering
Pre-filter vs post-filter matters: post-filtering after top-k can return zero results for selective filters. Check how your engine handles filtered ANN.
Quantization
Scalar/product/binary quantization cuts memory 4–32× with modest recall loss. The difference between a $400 and a $4,000 monthly bill at scale.
Freshness & deletes
Upserts and deletes in ANN indexes are messy (tombstones, segment merges). Know your engine's consistency lag, it's your stale-answer window.
Multi-tenancy
Namespace-per-tenant or partition keys; never rely on 'the filter in the prompt' for isolation. Tenant leakage via vector search is a real incident class.
mistakes: Buying a dedicated vector DB for 200K vectors that fit in pgvector
Never measuring recall of the ANN index against exact search
Post-filtering selective metadata → empty result sets
Treating the vector DB as source of truth, no rebuild path
Ignoring index rebuild/merge windows in latency SLOs
flags: "We chose it because it was on Hacker News", no requirements analysis
"Recall? It returns 10 results, so it works", accuracy never measured
"Rebuilding the index takes a week and we're scared", no automation
ask: How many vectors now, and at 10× growth?
What's measured ANN recall vs exact search?
How long until an updated doc is searchable?
Could pgvector do this and remove a system?

MODULES.title: Memory Systems
MODULES.tag: State across the stateless: sessions, users, agents
MODULES.why: The model forgets everything between calls. Every product experience of 'it remembers me', and every agent that survives a long task, is a memory system you engineered and own.
MODULES.mental: Memory is a write-path problem disguised as a read-path problem. Anyone can retrieve notes. The hard part is deciding what's worth writing, updating, or deleting without poisoning future behavior.
concepts: Memory taxonomy
Working memory (current context), episodic (past conversations/events), semantic (facts about user/domain), procedural (learned how-tos, feedback). Different storage and retrieval for each.
Short-term: history management
Sliding window + progressive summarization of older turns. Compaction summaries are lossy, pin durable facts elsewhere.
Long-term: extract-then-store
After conversations, extract candidate facts ('user is vegetarian'), dedupe against existing memory, store with provenance and timestamps. Retrieval-inject relevant memories per request.
File-based agent memory
The 2026 agent pattern: memory as plain files the agent reads/writes (progress notes, MEMORY.md indexes, scratchpads). Durable, inspectable, harness-portable, and it survives compaction.
Memory hygiene
Update beats append: contradictions must overwrite, not coexist. TTLs and decay for stale facts. User-visible and editable memory is both a trust and a correctness feature.
Memory poisoning
Bad writes compound: one wrong extracted 'fact' or an injected instruction stored as memory corrupts every future session. Validate writes; treat memory content as untrusted input on read.
Tooling
Mem0, Zep, LangMem, or in-house extract+vector store. The frameworks are thin; the design decisions (what to write, when to forget) are yours either way.
mistakes: Appending forever, context bloat and contradiction soup
Storing raw transcripts as 'memory' instead of extracted facts
No provenance, can't debug why the agent 'believes' something
Letting retrieved memory carry instructions (injection via memory)
No user visibility/control over what's remembered
flags: "The agent remembers wrong things and we can't fix it", no update/delete path
"Memory is the last 50 messages", that's history, not memory
"We store everything users say", privacy incident pending
ask: What decides whether something gets written to memory?
How do contradictions get resolved?
Can a user see and edit what's remembered?
Is memory content sanitized before re-entering context?

MODULES.title: AI Agents
MODULES.tag: LLMs in a loop with tools: capable, over-applied, and dependent on the harness
MODULES.why: Agents are the pattern everyone reaches for right now, and the one people misuse most. Knowing when a plain workflow beats an agent, and what actually makes agents reliable, is senior-level judgment.
MODULES.mental: An agent is an LLM in a while-loop with tools and a goal. The model decides, acts via a tool, observes the result, and repeats. Reliability comes from how you engineer that loop (the harness), not from the model being clever. Error compounds at every step: 95% per-step success works out to roughly 36% over 20 steps.
concepts: Workflow vs agent

Workflow: predefined steps with LLM calls inside (predictable, debuggable, cheap). Agent: model chooses the path (flexible, expensive, harder to bound). Default to workflows; earn your way to agents when paths can't be enumerated.
The agentic loop
Gather context → plan → act (tool call) → observe → verify → repeat or finish. Verification (tests, checks, self-review) is what separates demos from production.
Error compounding
Per-step reliability is everything. Mitigations: fewer steps, verification gates, checkpoints/rollback, human approval on irreversible actions.
Stopping conditions
Max iterations, budget caps, goal tests, and 'declare victory' detection. Agents fail both ways: giving up early and declaring premature success.
Granular tools beat clever prompts
Agents improve more from better tool design (clear names, descriptions, narrow scopes, good error messages) than from prompt tuning.
Human-in-the-loop
Approval gates on destructive/irreversible actions (sends, deletes, payments). Autonomy is a dial set per action class, not a switch.
Observability
Full traces of every step: model calls, tool I/O, decisions. Without traces, agent debugging is archaeology.
mistakes: Building an agent where a 5-step workflow would do
No iteration/budget caps, runaway loops burn real money
Letting agents take irreversible actions without gates
20 vague tools instead of 8 sharp ones
No verification step, trusting the model's claim of success
Debugging from final output instead of traces
flags: "It works in the demo", n=1, happy path
"The agent decides everything", autonomy without bounds or audit
"We can't reproduce failures", no tracing
ask: Why an agent and not a workflow here?
What bounds the loop, iterations, budget, time?
Which actions require human approval?
Show me the trace of the last failure.

MODULES.title: Tool / Function Calling
MODULES.tag: The hands of the model: API design for a probabilistic caller
MODULES.why: Tool calling is how models reach into the world. Most so-called agent bugs are really tool-design bugs: vague descriptions, leaky abstractions, errors that explain nothing.
MODULES.mental: Writing tool definitions is API design where the client is a probabilistic intern: brilliant, but easily confused. Use crisp names, unambiguous parameters, examples inside the descriptions, and error messages that teach. The model rereads your docs on every single call.
concepts: Mechanics

You send tool schemas (name, description, JSON params) with the request; model returns a structured tool_use call; YOUR code executes it; you return the result; model continues. The model never executes anything, it only asks.
Description quality
The description is a mini-prompt. Say what the tool does, when to use it, when NOT to, units/formats, and give an example. Most tool-selection errors trace to vague descriptions.
Tool scope
Match granularity to intent: a search_flights tool, not raw_sql_query. Too broad invites misuse; too narrow forces long chains. Consolidate related operations.
Error returns
Errors go back INTO context, make them instructive: 'date must be YYYY-MM-DD' beats 'Error 400'. The model self-corrects from good errors and flails on bad ones.
Parallel & forced calls
Independent calls batch in one turn (parallel) for latency wins. tool_choice can force a specific tool, handy for routing and structured extraction.
MCP
Model Context Protocol: open standard (now industry-wide) for exposing tools/resources to any model, write a server once, every harness can use it. The USB-C of tool calling.
Security
Tool calls are attacker-reachable surface: validate args server-side, enforce authz per call (the MODEL is not a principal), idempotency keys on mutations, allowlists over open-ended execution.
mistakes: Descriptions written for humans who already know the system
Returning raw stack traces or empty errors to the model
Trusting model-supplied args without server-side validation
One mega-tool with a 'command' string param, un-promptable
Ignoring parallel calls, serial latency stacks
flags: "The model keeps picking the wrong tool", read your descriptions aloud
"We pass user_id as a tool parameter", model-supplied identity = privilege escalation
"Adding a tool means redeploying everything", consider MCP
ask: Could a new hire pick the right tool from these descriptions alone?
Where is authorization enforced, the tool boundary or model side?
Which tools mutate state, and what makes them safe to retry?

MODULES.title: MCP Engineering
MODULES.tag: The port between agents and everything else, rewritten stateless in July 2026
MODULES.why: MCP stopped being a vendor protocol in December 2025, when Anthropic donated it to the Agentic AI Foundation, a Linux Foundation directed fund co-founded with Block and OpenAI and backed by Google, Microsoft, AWS and Cloudflare. It ships in ChatGPT, Cursor, Gemini, Copilot and VS Code, so it is the one integration skill that transfers across every harness you might be hired into. Then on 2026-07-28 the spec rewrote its own core, no handshake, no sessions, no server-initiated requests, and knowing which parts were removed outright versus merely deprecated is the difference between a two-day migration and a week of confused debugging.
MODULES.mental: MCP is the USB port between agents and everything else. USB didn't make peripherals better, it made them universal: one plug, any host, no bespoke driver per laptop. Write one server, every compliant harness can use it. And the analogy holds all the way down, because the port is also the attack surface, anything you plug in runs inside your trust boundary and its tool descriptions are prompt content you never wrote.
concepts: Where MCP sits

Raw tool calling is your process calling your function, in one codebase. MCP is a JSON-RPC protocol between a client (inside the harness) and a server (a separate process you launch, or an HTTP endpoint you call) that exposes capabilities to any compliant client. A2A is the layer above: MCP is how an agent uses its hands, A2A is how two agents shake them.
The three primitives

Tools are model-controlled (API calls, writes). Resources are application-controlled (file contents, git history, anything the harness attaches). Prompts are user-controlled (slash commands, menu options). That control hierarchy is the design question for every capability you expose, and it is unchanged in the 2026-07-28 revision.
The stateless core (2026-07-28)

The current protocol version. SEP-2575 removed the initialize / notifications-initialized handshake; SEP-2567 removed protocol-level sessions and the Mcp-Session-Id header. Every request now carries io.modelcontextprotocol/protocolVersion and io.modelcontextprotocol/clientCapabilities in _meta, and servers needing cross-call state mint their own handles and pass them back as ordinary tool arguments.
Removed vs deprecated

The single most important distinction in this revision. Removed outright, no window: the handshake, sessions/Mcp-Session-Id, ping, logging/setLevel, notifications/roots/list_changed, the HTTP GET stream, resources/subscribe and unsubscribe, SSE resumability. Deprecated but still functional: Roots, Sampling, Logging (SEP-2577) and Dynamic Client Registration, under SEP-2596's twelve-month floor, earliest removal being the first revision released on or after 2027-07-28.
MRTR

Multi Round-Trip Requests (SEP-2322) replaced server-initiated requests, which the spec calls a breaking change. Instead of calling the client, the server returns resultType: "input_required" with an inputRequests map and an opaque requestState; the client gathers the input and retries the ORIGINAL request, under a new JSON-RPC id, carrying inputResponses. Only prompts/get, resources/read and tools/call may do this.
Transports and header routing

stdio: the client launches your server as a subprocess, newline-delimited JSON-RPC over stdin/stdout, stderr free for logging. Streamable HTTP: one POST endpoint, one message per POST, answered with JSON or a request-scoped SSE stream. New in 2026-07-28, HTTP requests mirror routing into headers (MCP-Protocol-Version, Mcp-Method, plus Mcp-Name on tools/call, resources/read and prompts/get) so gateways route without parsing bodies; a header/body mismatch MUST be rejected with 400 and JSON-RPC error -32020.
Authorization: CIMD

Client ID Metadata Documents make the client_id an HTTPS URL, with a path, that resolves to a JSON metadata document declaring that same client_id plus client_name and redirect_uris. The win is portability, one identity across authorization servers with no re-registration. Priority order: pre-registered credentials, then CIMD if the AS advertises it, then DCR if it advertises a registration endpoint, then prompt the user. DCR is deprecated, not removed.
Discovery and cacheable lists

Servers MUST implement server/discover, which returns supported versions, capabilities and identity in one round trip and doubles as the client's backward-compatibility probe on stdio. Three outcomes: a DiscoverResult means modern; UnsupportedProtocolVersionError means modern on a version you don't speak, and falling back to initialize is explicitly wrong; anything else means legacy. SEP-2549 adds ttlMs and cacheScope to list results and resources/read, and servers SHOULD return tools/list in deterministic order so prompt caches hit.
Consuming servers is a supply-chain decision

Installing a third-party server means running someone else's code and injecting their prose into your model's context. OWASP's MCP Top 10 names the failure modes: MCP03 Tool Poisoning, MCP04 Supply Chain and Dependency Tampering, MCP09 Shadow MCP Servers, MCP01 Token Mismanagement. Pin versions, review the tool descriptions the way you'd review a system prompt, re-diff them on every upgrade, and keep credentials in a vault injected at execution time, never in arguments or descriptions.
When NOT to build a server

MCP earns its keep when a capability crosses a boundary, another team, another harness, another vendor's client. One consumer inside one codebase does not clear that bar: you'd be buying a second process, a transport, an auth story and a supply-chain question in exchange for reuse that doesn't exist. Ship the plain function tool, and promote it to a server the day the second consumer appears.
mistakes: Writing to the initialize handshake in 2026, it was removed outright and fails at first contact
Reading 'deprecated' as 'gone': Roots, Sampling, Logging and DCR still work, with a floor of 2027-07-28
Keeping cross-call state in memory keyed by something the protocol no longer hands you
Redeeming requestState without verifying it, it round-trips through the client and is attacker-controlled
Installing registry servers unpinned, then never re-diffing tool descriptions on upgrade
Quoting MCP adoption percentages from SEO blogs in a design doc, the registry exposes no corpus total and third-party counts differ by an order of magnitude
Standing up a protocol server for a capability with exactly one consumer in one codebase
flags: "Just call initialize first", that handshake was removed in 2026-07-28, not deprecated
"We key the user off the session id", there are no protocol sessions any more
"We npx the server straight from the registry", unpinned tool descriptions are prompt content nobody reviewed
"The server can borrow our model via sampling", deprecated, and always someone else's trust boundary and inference bill
ask: Which protocol version does our server/discover advertise, and which do our clients actually speak?
Where does cross-call state live now that sessions are gone, and what stops a client forging the handle?
Who reviews a third-party server's tool descriptions, and what happens when they change on upgrade?
Does this capability cross a boundary, or is a plain function tool enough?
What in our servers is on the deprecation clock, and what's the date?

MODULES.title: Agent Harnesses
MODULES.tag: The scaffolding around the model: 2026's defining layer
MODULES.why: The same model scores wildly differently depending on its harness. In Princeton HAL's CORE-Bench evaluations (Dec 2025), Claude Opus 4.5 scored ~78% under a Claude Code-based scaffold versus 42% under the generic CORE-Agent scaffold, a ~36-point gap from the same model. Anthropic's own Opus 4.8 release confirmed the pattern: Terminal-Bench scores differ significantly depending on which harness you use. In 2026, harness engineering is AI engineering. It's where capability actually comes from.
MODULES.mental: If the model is the CPU, the harness is the operating system. It curates context (RAM), runs the boot sequence (system prompt, hooks), provides drivers (tools, skills), schedules work (loops, sub-agents), and handles persistence (memory, compaction). Same CPU, different OS, wildly different machine.
concepts: What a harness is

Everything wrapping the model call in an agentic system: system prompt assembly, tool registry, the loop, context management (compaction, pruning), permissions/approvals, tracing, error recovery, checkpoints/resume. The model proposes; the harness disposes.
The 2026 landscape

Claude Code / Claude Agent SDK (the harness behind Claude Code, opened up for custom agents), OpenAI Agents SDK (major April 15, 2026 upgrade: in-distribution harness with Codex-style tools, sandboxed execution, long-horizon memory), LangGraph (explicit graph orchestration), plus lighter frameworks (CrewAI, Strands, Smolagents). Snapshot verified Aug 9, 2026.
Harness > model deltas

On multi-step tasks, harness quality swamps model differences. Benchmark results are model+harness results. When comparing models, hold the harness constant; when buying capability, evaluate the harness first.
Context management core

The harness's main job: what enters the window each turn. Compaction of old turns, pruning stale tool output, JIT retrieval, sub-agents with fresh windows for noisy subtasks, cache-friendly stable→volatile layout.
Long-running agents

Work spans many context windows; each session 'wakes up' amnesiac. Anthropic's proven pattern: an initializer agent sets up the environment (init script, feature list as structured JSON, initial commit), then each coding session reads progress notes + git log, picks ONE feature, verifies end-to-end, commits, updates the progress file. Artifacts on disk bridge the amnesia.
Failure modes harnesses fix

One-shotting (doing too much, dying mid-task with undocumented state) → incremental feature-at-a-time. Premature victory ('looks done!') → explicit pass/fail feature checklist the agent may only flip after verification. Broken-state handoffs → commit clean, log progress, boot-check before new work.
Hooks, permissions, sandboxing

Production harnesses expose hooks (pre/post tool-call interception), permission tiers per tool/action, and sandboxed execution (filesystem/network isolation) so the agent can act boldly inside a safe boundary.
Skills & extensibility
Harnesses load capability packs at runtime: skills (instructions + scripts loaded JIT), MCP servers (external tools), sub-agent definitions. Capability becomes configuration, not code change.
Build vs adopt

Adopt a proven harness (Claude Agent SDK, OpenAI Agents SDK, LangGraph) unless you have hard requirements they can't meet. In-house harnesses recreate years of loop/compaction/permission engineering, usually badly.
mistakes: Evaluating models without controlling for harness, you benchmarked the scaffolding
Prompting 'build the whole app' instead of structuring incremental, verifiable units
Letting agents mark work done without an end-to-end verification step
Relying on compaction alone for long-task state instead of durable artifacts (progress files, git)
Building a bespoke harness for problems the Agent SDK solved in 2025
No resume capability, a crash at hour 6 restarts at hour 0
flags: "We wrote our own agent loop in a weekend", wait for the compaction, permissions, and resume bugs
"The agent says it finished", does anything verify that claim?
"Long tasks mysteriously degrade", context rot, no pruning/compaction strategy
"We switched models and everything broke", harness was overfit to one provider
ask: What's our harness, and why this one?
How does state survive a context-window boundary or crash?
What verifies a step before the agent moves on?
Which actions are sandboxed vs gated on human approval?
If the model improves 20%, what in our harness captures that gain?

MODULES.title: Multi-Agent Systems
MODULES.tag: When one context window isn't enough, and the coordination tax that follows
MODULES.why: Multi-agent works well for parallelizable, context-heavy jobs and wastes money everywhere else. The skill is telling the two apart and paying the coordination tax only when it buys you something.
MODULES.mental: Multi-agent is an org chart for context windows. You hire another agent for the same reason you hire another person: the work is too big for one head. And like any org, every added agent brings communication overhead, drift risk, and cost. Headcount has to justify itself.
concepts: Why split
Context isolation (a noisy subtask pollutes the main window), parallelism (independent subtasks fan out), specialization (different tools/prompts per role). NOT because it sounds sophisticated.
Orchestrator–worker
The proven pattern: a lead agent decomposes the task, spawns workers with focused briefs and fresh contexts, integrates results. Workers return conclusions, not transcripts.
Handoff quality
Agents communicate through text briefs. Vague briefs → drifted work, duplicated effort. The orchestrator's brief-writing quality is the system's bottleneck, same as human delegation.
Sub-agents as context tools
The most defensible 2026 use: spawn a fresh-window sub-agent to do a broad noisy search/analysis and return a tight summary. Pure context hygiene.
Cost multiplier
Multi-agent systems can burn 4–15× the tokens of single-agent on the same task. Reserve for tasks where the value or parallelism justifies it.
Shared state
Filesystem/artifacts beat message-passing for cross-agent state (durable, inspectable). Concurrent writes need ownership rules, last-write-wins eats work.
Debugging
One bad handoff cascades. Trace per-agent AND cross-agent; evaluate the system end-to-end, not just each agent in isolation.
mistakes: Five agents role-playing a company to do one agent's job
Workers inheriting the orchestrator's entire context, no isolation benefit
Two agents editing the same artifact without ownership rules
Evaluating agents individually, never the integrated outcome
Ignoring the token bill until finance asks
flags: "We have a researcher, writer, critic, editor, and manager agent" for a task one good prompt handles
"Results vary wildly run to run", handoff briefs too vague
"It costs $4 per request", coordination tax nobody priced
ask: What does splitting buy here, isolation, parallelism, or specialization?
What exactly does a worker receive in its brief?
What's the token cost multiple vs single-agent?
How do we evaluate the end-to-end output?

MODULES.title: AI System Design
MODULES.tag: The full production stack around the model call
MODULES.why: The model call is 5% of the system. Gateways, caching, queues, fallbacks, observability, and cost controls are the other 95%, and they're what page you at 3am.
MODULES.mental: Design AI systems like distributed systems with a flaky, expensive, slow dependency at the core. Every classic pattern applies (timeouts, retries, fallbacks, circuit breakers, queues, caches), plus new ones: token budgets, eval gates, and semantic caching.
concepts: LLM gateway
Single choke point for all model traffic: routing, fallback, retries, rate limiting, caching, cost attribution, key management. LiteLLM, Portkey, Kong AI, or in-house. Non-negotiable beyond one team.
Fallback chains
Primary model → secondary provider → degraded mode (cached/templated response). Providers have multi-hour outages regularly; design for it.
Caching layers
Prompt caching (provider-side prefix), exact-match response cache, semantic cache (embedding-similarity hit on paraphrases). Order-of-magnitude cost/latency wins on repetitive traffic.
Async by default
Anything not interactive goes through queues + batch APIs (50% discount). Reserve synchronous capacity for user-facing paths; stream everything interactive.
Cost architecture
Token metering per feature/user/route, budgets with alerts, tier routing (cheap model first, escalate on need), max_tokens caps everywhere. Cost is a first-class SLO.
Observability
Traces for every call (prompt, params, tokens, latency, cost), eval scores on sampled production traffic, drift dashboards. LangSmith, Langfuse, Braintrust, Arize Phoenix, or OTel GenAI conventions.
Guardrail placement

Input rails (injection screens, PII redaction, topic filters) → model → output rails (schema validation, grounding checks, safety filters). Rails are cheap small-model or rule passes, not flagship calls.
Versioned everything
Prompts, model IDs, tool schemas, eval sets, pinned and versioned together. 'The model updated and behavior changed' should be a deliberate event, not a surprise.
mistakes: Calling provider SDKs directly from app code, no gateway
Synchronous calls for batch-shaped work at 2× the price
No per-feature cost attribution until the bill doubles
Retrying non-idempotent agent actions blindly
Pinning nothing, silent model/prompt drift
One global rate limit shared by interactive and batch traffic
flags: "The AI bill surprised us", no metering or budgets
"Provider outage = our outage", no fallback chain
"We found out from users", no eval sampling on prod traffic
ask: What happens, step by step, when the primary provider goes down?
What's cost per request by route, and who watches it?
What % of traffic could move to batch/async?
Where are the guardrails, and what do they catch monthly?

MODULES.title: Evaluation & Eval Harnesses
MODULES.tag: The discipline that separates shipping from guessing
MODULES.why: Probabilistic systems can't be unit-tested into correctness. Evals are how you know quality went up, catch regressions before users do, and ship prompt or model changes with evidence. Teams without evals are flying IFR with no instruments.
MODULES.mental: Evals are the test suite for behavior: golden datasets are your fixtures, scorers are your assertions, the eval harness is your CI. No eval, no deploy, exactly like no tests, no merge.
concepts: The eval stack

Golden dataset (curated input→expected pairs, grown from real failures) → scorers (exact match, rubric, model-graded) → harness (runs the suite, reports, gates CI) → production sampling (online evals on live traffic).
LLM-as-judge

A model grades outputs against a rubric. Now standard practice, near-human agreement when configured well. Rules: binary judgments beat 1–10 scales, one criterion per judge call, calibrate against human labels periodically, and never let the generating model grade itself ungated.
Eval harness tooling (2026)

promptfoo (open-source CLI, declarative configs, CI-native, red-teaming built in), Braintrust (managed: instrument→observe→annotate→evaluate→deploy, PR regression comments), LangSmith, DeepEval, Arize Phoenix. Pick one that gates releases, evals that don't block ships are decoration.
Agentic evals

Score trajectories, not just final answers: did it pick sensible tools, recover from errors, stop appropriately? Plus end-state verification (tests pass, artifact correct). Much harder than single-turn, and where harness quality shows up.
Component + end-to-end
RAG: eval retrieval (recall@k) separately from generation (faithfulness, relevance). Agents: per-step success AND task completion. Component evals localize blame; end-to-end evals tell the truth.
Online evals
Sample production traffic, score asynchronously (cheap judge model), alert on drift. Your eval set is always stale; production is the real distribution.
Failure-driven datasets
Every production failure becomes an eval case. The golden set should grow weekly. 50 hard, real cases beat 5,000 synthetic ones.
Red-teaming
Adversarial evals: injection attempts, jailbreaks, PII extraction, off-policy requests. promptfoo and dedicated suites automate this; run it like security scanning, on schedule.
Error bars on evals

A 2-point gain on a 200-case suite is usually noise, not progress: before celebrating a delta, ask whether it clears a confidence interval, and remember that detecting small real differences takes hundreds to thousands of cases. Anthropic's 'Adding Error Bars to Evals' is the canonical treatment, significance tests on eval deltas, sample-size math, clustered standard errors when cases share a source. If you can't say whether a delta beats noise, you don't have a measurement, you have a mood.
mistakes: Vibes-driven iteration, 'it seems better' is not a metric
1–10 judge scales (noisy) instead of binary/categorical rubrics
Eval set frozen at launch while traffic distribution moves
Testing only happy paths, no adversarial or edge cases
Evals exist but don't gate deploys
Same model generates and judges with no calibration check
flags: "How do you know the new prompt is better?" → silence
"We eval before big releases", should be every change, in CI
"Our success metric is thumbs-up rate", biased, sparse, lagging
ask: Show me the eval run for the last prompt change.
How many cases, and when did the golden set last grow?
What's judge agreement with human labels?
What samples production, and what alerted last month?

MODULES.title: Hallucination & Guardrails
MODULES.tag: Confidently wrong: engineering around the failure mode that erodes trust
MODULES.why: Hallucination is intrinsic to next-token prediction. The model is rewarded for sounding fluent, not for being true. One confidently wrong answer in a legal, medical, or financial flow can erase the product's credibility. You can't eliminate it, so you have to engineer around it.
MODULES.mental: Treat every model output as a claim from a brilliant, eager intern with no fear of being wrong. Trust grows only through grounding (citations to sources), verification (checks against truth), and constraint (schemas, allowed values). The system, not the model, is what makes answers trustworthy.
concepts: Why models hallucinate
Next-token training optimizes plausibility, not truth; the model has no internal fact/fiction boundary. Worst in: niche facts, citations, numbers, recent events, and anything beyond its data.
Grounding via RAG

Force answers from retrieved sources with chunk-level citations. 'Answer only from the provided context; say I don't know otherwise', then VERIFY citations exist and support the claim (entailment check).
Faithfulness scoring
An LLM-judge or NLI model checks: is each claim in the answer entailed by the retrieved context? Gate or flag low-faithfulness answers. This is the workhorse production defense.
Structured constraint
Schemas, enums, and allowed-value lists shrink the hallucination surface: a model can't invent a product ID if output is constrained to retrieved IDs.
Abstention design
'I don't know' must be an acceptable, rewarded output path, in prompts, in UX, in evals. Systems that punish abstention manufacture hallucinations.
Prompt injection

The other trust failure: instructions hidden in retrieved docs, emails, or web pages hijack the model. Treat ALL external content as untrusted data: delimit it, instruct the model it's data-not-commands, strip suspicious patterns, and never let injected content trigger privileged tool calls without checks.
Layered guardrails
Input rails (injection screens, PII, topic) → grounded generation → output rails (schema, faithfulness, safety, allowed-claims). Each layer cheap; defense in depth.
UX honesty
Show sources, confidence cues, and easy escalation to humans. Calibrated trust beats blind trust, design for verification, not authority.
mistakes: Asking the model 'are you sure?' as the verification strategy
Citations displayed but never validated against content
Prompts that forbid 'I don't know', abstention punished
Retrieved/email/web content concatenated raw into context (injection highway)
Guardrails only on output, input rails missing
Treating low hallucination on a benchmark as product safety
flags: "The model cited a case/paper that doesn't exist" and nothing caught it
"Users found the wrong answers", no faithfulness gate
"An email told the agent to forward the inbox and it did", no injection defense on tool-using agents
ask: What checks an answer's claims against its sources?
What happens when the model should say 'I don't know'?
How is retrieved/external content sanitized before the model sees it?
Which guardrail fired most last month, and on what?

MODULES.title: Leadership Playbook
MODULES.tag: Judgment, communication, and the meta-skill of staying current
MODULES.why: Past senior level, your value comes from decisions and narratives: which bets to make, what to tell executives, how to grow a team's AI judgment. Technical depth is the entry fee. This is the differentiator.
MODULES.mental: Your job is portfolio management of irreversibility. Let teams move fast on reversible decisions (prompts, models behind a gateway, retrieval tuning), and slow down hard on one-way doors: data contracts, vendor lock-in, trust-destroying launches, harness rewrites.
concepts: Build/buy/wait

Buy commodity (gateways, vector DBs, eval platforms, harnesses), build differentiation (domain evals, data pipelines, product UX), wait on hype (most multi-agent, most fine-tuning). Revisit quarterly, 'wait' answers expire.
The demo-to-prod gap
Demos are the happy path at n=1. Production is adversarial users, edge cases, cost at scale, and 99.5% reliability targets. Budget 3–10× the demo effort; say this out loud at kickoff.
Executive translation

Frame AI work in risk/cost/revenue, not architecture. 'Faithfulness gating cut wrong-answer escalations 40%' lands; 'we added an NLI entailment check' doesn't. Always pair capability claims with their failure modes.
ROI discipline
Cost per task × volume vs human-time saved or revenue created, tracked post-launch, not just projected. Kill features whose unit economics never close.
Team capability

Grow evals-first culture: every engineer writes eval cases; failures become test cases; demos require eval scores. Hire for systems thinking and judgment over framework familiarity, frameworks churn quarterly.
Responsible deployment
Know your obligations: data residency, PII handling, provenance/disclosure of AI content, human override on consequential decisions, audit trails. Governance done early is cheap; retrofitted, brutal.
Staying current sustainably

The field turns over quarterly. Protocol: one deep re-implementation per month beats ten skimmed posts; maintain your own eval set to test new models in an afternoon; follow primary sources (provider engineering blogs, model cards) over commentary.
mistakes: Letting teams build agents before evals exist, backwards
Announcing capabilities to execs without failure modes attached
Treating model choice as permanent (it's a gateway config) while treating data contracts as casual (they're forever)
Hiring framework experts over systems thinkers
Measuring activity (features shipped) over outcomes (task success, unit economics)
flags: "We don't have time for evals this quarter", you don't have time NOT to
"The vendor says it's 99% accurate", on whose data?
"We'll add governance after launch", translation: after the incident
ask: Which of our current decisions are one-way doors?
What would falsify our success claim for this feature?
If the flagship model gets 30% better next quarter, what do we delete?
Who on the team can challenge a vendor benchmark with our own numbers?

MODULES.title: The Hiring Loop
MODULES.tag: Assembling everything you've built into offers, round by round
MODULES.why: AI Engineer is LinkedIn's #1 fastest-growing US title (postings up 143% year over year, ~43,500 of them), but fewer candidates get hired per role, so the screening bar rose and tolerance for a borderline round dropped. Everything earlier in this course is the material. This module is the assembly: the artifacts each round scores, and the reps that make them yours.
MODULES.mental: Interviewing in 2026 is an evidence problem, not a knowledge problem. Every round asks one question in different clothes: have you shipped an AI system, and do you know exactly where it breaks? Arrive with the evidence pre-built, a deployed URL, eval numbers, a trace you actually debugged, a trade-off you would now reverse, so nobody has to take your word for anything.
concepts: The consolidated five-round loop

Theory screen, coding round, project deep-dive, AI system design, behavioral. Reported 2026 topic mix runs ~40% RAG/evals/agents, 30% production systems, 20% LLM internals, 10% behavioral. Design used to be a senior gate; it now appears at mid and even entry level as its own 35–60 minute conversation.
Two coding modes, both rehearsed

AI-assisted rounds are real: Google is piloting one with an approved assistant for junior and mid US roles, plus a code-comprehension round where you read, debug, and optimize an existing codebase with Gemini available. Take-homes at Stripe, Shopify, Vercel and most YC-stage startups assume AI use. Standardized Google/Meta/Amazon loops still run AI-off algorithm rounds. Practice both, they score different muscles.
Judging code beats producing it

In assisted rounds the scored skill flipped from writing to evaluating. The fastest rejection in the format is accepting a plausible-but-wrong suggestion without reading it. Narrate the review out loud: what you checked, what you rejected, why. 'Do you use AI?' is a real question now, and the answer that lands names a tool, a use, and the last time it was wrong.
Eval-first take-homes

Roughly a third of companies with disclosed processes use a take-home; assignments skew RAG (40%+) and agentic (30%+), windows run 2–7 days, and a live follow-up discussion is now part of the format because AI-generated submissions made the artifact alone uninformative. Build order is the signal: golden set first, then code. YC startups name 'didn't start with evals' as an explicit red flag.
The failing-trace round

You get handed a broken trace and asked to diagnose it: runaway tool calls, retrieval drift, a prompt regression, a multi-agent loop that quietly left the plan. Agents fail in ways ordinary test suites never catch, which is why this round exists. What's scored is discipline, not speed: read before theorizing, isolate the first bad step, name the telemetry that should have caught it.
AI system design as a timed scenario

35–60 minutes, open-ended: a RAG pipeline, an agentic architecture, or an eval methodology, with production safety folded in. Interviewers probe chunking strategy, embedding and reranker choice, retrieval scoring, and whether you know what a token costs at scale. Requirements and eval plan first; candidates who open by drawing boxes lose the round in its opening minutes.
The deep-dive narrative arc

Motivation, problem, approach, what broke, trade-offs, impact with metrics. The 'what broke' beat is the round. Interviewers stopped asking what agents could do and started asking what you shipped and where it failed, so a story that ends at 'it worked' reads as something you read about rather than built.
Portfolio truth

One deployed URL plus eval metrics plus an architecture README is verifiable in about 60 seconds, and it outranks a fine-tuned model with no live endpoint, the explicitly named loser. Proctored and project-based certs (AWS, Azure, GCP, DeepLearning.AI) still earn ATS keywords and give study structure. Video-completion badges are ignored.
mistakes: Describing what agents could do instead of what yours actually broke on
Writing take-home code before the eval set, the exact sequence YC startups name as a red flag
Leading the portfolio with a fine-tuned model that has no live endpoint and no measured number
Rehearsing one coding mode, the market runs assisted rounds and AI-off algorithm rounds side by side
Accepting an assistant's plausible suggestion unread while the interviewer watches you not read it
Marketing a completion badge as the credential when the deployed capstone is the credential
flags: "We used LLM-as-judge and it looked good", on whose labels, calibrated how?
"First I'd pick a vector database", the eval set comes first, and the interviewer is timing that instinct
"I don't really use AI tools", in 2026 that reads as unexamined, not principled
"It's about 95% accurate", on which set, measured when, against what baseline?
ask: Which round of this loop would I fail today, and what artifact fixes it?
Can a stranger verify my best project in 60 seconds without me in the room?
What does one request in my capstone cost, and can I say the number out loud?
When did I last catch an AI assistant being confidently wrong, and how did I catch it?

MODULES.title: Fine-Tuning & Alignment Mechanics
MODULES.tag: When to reshape weights vs when to reshape prompts, and how not to wreck the model
MODULES.why: At volume, fine-tuning buys you unit economics and behavioral consistency that prompting can't reach. A mis-scoped fine-tune does the opposite: it destroys general capabilities, quietly inflates eval scores, and costs you weeks to recover from. Staff-level judgment is knowing when the math works, and knowing when to stop before the damage compounds.
MODULES.mental: Fine-tuning is surgery on the weight space; prompting is clothing. Both change outputs, but surgery is permanent. You can re-dress a model in 30 seconds. You cannot un-train it on bad data. The decision rule: if a prompted baseline with good few-shot examples hits acceptable quality, skip the surgery. Reach for fine-tuning only when you have a volume, latency, or consistency problem that prompting can't solve, a clean labeled dataset, and a regression suite ready to run the moment training finishes.
concepts: When fine-tuning beats prompting

Four specific signals: (1) volume, few-shot tokens at 500K req/day cost more than amortized training; (2) latency, eliminating a 2K-token few-shot block cuts TTFT materially; (3) consistency, behavioral style the model drifts from under prompt variation; (4) capability gap, an output format or skill the model genuinely doesn't have. Absent at least one, stop and improve prompts.
LoRA mechanics

Low-rank decomposition: freeze W (d×k), learn ΔW = A×B where A is d×r and B is r×k, r << min(d,k). Trainable params ≈ 0.5–1% of the full model. Rank r=8–16 for style tasks; r=32–64 for new capabilities. The key insight: model behavior lives in low-rank subspaces, you reshape the behavior without touching the knowledge-bearing full-rank weights. Alternatives worth knowing: DoRA (Weight-Decomposed LoRA) adds a magnitude component and often matches full fine-tune quality at r=8; IA3 (few-parameter prefix-style tuning) is even lighter and useful for style-only adaptation; full fine-tuning remains the ceiling on capability tasks when you have the GPU budget.
QLoRA

LoRA + 4-bit NF4-quantized base model. Runs a 7B fine-tune on one 24GB GPU where standard LoRA needs 80GB. Cost: ~2–4% quality loss vs full-precision LoRA, negligible for narrow tasks. The practical gate to fine-tuning without A100 budget.
DPO vs PPO/RLHF

DPO (Direct Preference Optimization): offline, labeled preference pairs (winner/loser), no reward model, no rollouts, trains directly on a Bradley-Terry objective. Simpler, often matches PPO on helpfulness. PPO: train a reward model on preferences, use RL to update the policy against it. Use PPO when your preference signal is complex, conditional, or must generalize to unseen domains; use DPO otherwise.
What RLHF changes in production

RLHF shapes the behavioral envelope, refusal tone, calibrated hedging, helpfulness style, not raw capability. Capability comes from pretraining. In production, RLHF-tuned models can be LESS capable on specific tasks where safety filters or refusal tendencies fire. Fine-tuning on top of an instruct model without instruction-following examples can erode RLHF alignment.
Catastrophic forgetting

Continuous fine-tuning overwrites pretraining weight patterns. Mitigations: conservative learning rate for LoRA (1e-4–2e-4 is the standard LoRA range; never use the default Adam lr of 1e-3 with LoRA, it's too high and causes instability); small, clean dataset (less gradient signal); LoRA itself (base frozen by construction); replay (mix 5–10% general pretraining-style samples into the fine-tune batch).
Base vs instruct model selection

Instruct model: add a new capability while keeping alignment, the common case. Base model: run a full preference pipeline (SFT → RM → PPO or SFT → DPO) from scratch, or when you need raw next-token completion behavior. Wrong choice: fine-tuning an instruct model on base-style text (no system/user role markup) strips the role-delimiter alignment it was built on.
Eval methodology for fine-tuned models

Hold-out test split must be drawn BEFORE any labeling or training work, contamination is invisible in loss curves and undetectable after the fact. Contamination signal: eval score suspiciously higher than prompted baseline by >5 points. Additionally: run a regression suite on 3–5 general tasks (instruction following, summarization, Q&A) before calling the fine-tune done.
The data quality bar

1,000–5,000 high-quality, consistent, edge-case-covering examples beat 100,000 noisy ones. Quality checklist: format consistency (same schema across all examples), factual accuracy (domain expert review), correct task behavior on hard cases, coverage of the failure modes you're trying to fix. Manual review of at least 200 examples is not optional, loss curves cannot catch systematic label errors.
mistakes: Starting fine-tuning before prompt engineering is fully exhausted, almost always the wrong sequence
Training on a dataset nobody has manually reviewed, systematic label errors are invisible in training loss
Using the default Adam learning rate (1e-3) with LoRA, it is 5–10× too high for adapter training and causes instability and catastrophic forgetting; the correct LoRA range is 1e-4 to 2e-4
No held-out test set defined before training begins, contamination is undetectable after the fact
Measuring loss improvement instead of task metric improvement, the model can memorize format and score zero on content
Deploying without a general-capability regression suite, RLHF alignment damage often shows up in adjacent tasks
No version control for the fine-tuned model artifacts alongside the training data and eval set
flags: "We fine-tuned it and the loss went to near-zero", memorized the training set, not learned the task
"We're using all our production data as training data", no held-out split, contaminated eval
"We just need to fine-tune it a bit" before any eval set or labeled data exists
"Fine-tuning fixed the style" without testing whether it broke anything else
"We trained for 10 epochs to be safe", overfit; 2–3 epochs on clean data is almost always better
ask: What would a zero-shot or few-shot prompted baseline achieve, and what specific gap justifies fine-tuning?
What is in the training data, and who reviewed it manually?
Was the test split defined and frozen before any data labeling began?
What general-capability regression tests run after training, and what do they show?
What's the off-ramp plan if the fine-tuned model degrades on production metrics?

MODULES.title: AI Security & Adversarial Robustness
MODULES.tag: New attack surfaces, new attack classes: engineering a system that holds under adversarial pressure
MODULES.why: Every LLM feature you ship is a new attack surface. Prompt injection, jailbreaks, and supply-chain attacks buried in tool results are production incident classes, not theoretical worries. The threat model, the pre-launch red-team, and the defense architecture all land on the staff engineer, because no amount of vendor alignment makes a system safe without the structural controls you design yourself.
MODULES.mental: Your AI system is a trusted executive who reads every email, including the ones from attackers. Design as if the model cannot be made adversarially robust, because no model resists a sufficiently crafted attack. The controls that actually hold are structural: external content framed as untrusted data, privileged actions gated independently of anything the model read, and defense-in-depth that never relies on the model's judgment as the last line.
concepts: Direct prompt injection

User-supplied input that contains instructions overriding system behavior. The classic 'ignore prior instructions' family. Mechanically: the model has no instruction/data boundary in token space; it pattern-matches, and a well-crafted user message looks syntactically indistinguishable from a system instruction. Classifiers + positive framing ('your only job is X') reduce exposure; no prompt wording eliminates it.
Indirect prompt injection

Attacker-controlled content enters through the environment, retrieved documents, emails, web pages, tool results, not through the user's direct input. The agent reads it in the course of a legitimate task. This is an ambient attack requiring no malicious user. Higher severity for agents because tool results automatically carry execution context. In the 2025 OWASP list this is a subtype of LLM01 Prompt Injection, not a separate entry.
Multi-hop and multi-modal injection

Multi-hop: a payload planted in memory, a tool result, or an agent handoff activates in a later context. Multi-modal: hidden text in images (white-on-white, adversarial pixels encoding text, image metadata), instructions embedded in audio, or injections in retrieved documents containing figure OCR text.
Jailbreak pattern families

(1) Prompt wrapping: role-play framing ('pretend you have no restrictions'), fiction laundering ('write a story where a character explains…'); (2) Context inflation: gradually escalate from benign to harmful across a long conversation; (3) Encoding attacks: base64, ROT13, leetspeak to bypass keyword classifiers; (4) Many-shot jailbreaks (MSJA): include many examples of compliance before the harmful request, exploiting in-context learning to override alignment.
Structured red-team methodology

Threat model first: actor (curious user, external attacker, malicious insider, compromised upstream), motive, capability, entry point. Attack surface enumeration: every channel that feeds external content to the model. Manual probing (human red-teamers are more creative than any fuzzer). Automated sweep: promptfoo red-team mode with injection, jailbreak, and PII-extraction test suites; garak (NVIDIA, 120+ probe modules) and PyRIT (Microsoft, now at microsoft/PyRIT) round out the standard open-source stack. Run pre-launch and on schedule (quarterly minimum).
OWASP LLM Top 10 (2025) as a review checklist

LLM01 Prompt Injection (direct and indirect both live here), LLM02 Sensitive Information Disclosure, LLM03 Supply Chain, LLM04 Data and Model Poisoning, LLM05 Improper Output Handling (trusting model output as safe downstream), LLM06 Excessive Agency (agent takes irreversible actions without gates), LLM07 System Prompt Leakage, LLM08 Vector and Embedding Weaknesses, LLM09 Misinformation, LLM10 Unbounded Consumption (billion-token context attacks). Verified Aug 9, 2026. Walk through this list before any feature launches; for agents, pair it with the OWASP Top 10 for Agentic Applications for 2026 (ASI01–ASI10, from the Gen AI Security Project's Agentic Security Initiative, Dec 2025).
Supply chain risks

Malicious MCP server: returns injected instructions as tool results; the agent trusts them because tools are trusted callers. Poisoned embeddings: an embedding model backdoored during training can cause specific trigger phrases to retrieve malicious content. Compromised tool results: a legitimate API returning attacker-controlled content (open-redirect, response injection). Mitigation: pin MCP server versions; validate tool result structure; treat tool outputs as untrusted data.
MCP tool poisoning and rug pulls

Tool poisoning: an MCP server ships tool descriptions carrying hidden instructions, invisible in the client UI, fully visible to the model, injection through the tool schema itself (canonical write-up: Invariant Labs, Apr 2025). Rug pull: the server mutates its tool descriptions after you approved them, so the tool you audited is not the tool you're running. OWASP maps this to ASI04 Agentic Supply Chain. Mitigations: pin server versions and hash tool descriptions at approval, re-verify on any change, and apply OWASP's third-party MCP server cheatsheet.
Output filtering architecture

Input classifiers before the model: injection detection (classifier + regex heuristics), PII detection (NER-based), topic filters. Output classifiers after the model: schema validation, safety classifier, content policy check. Rule-based filters: fast, zero false negatives on exact patterns, brittle to paraphrase. Classifier-based: catches novel variants, higher latency, non-zero false positives. Both layers are required, neither alone is sufficient.
Guardrail model survey

Verified Aug 9, 2026: Llama Guard 4 (12B, natively multimodal, MLCommons hazard taxonomy) for content classification; Llama Prompt Guard 2 (86M/22M) for jailbreak and injection detection, the 22M variant cuts latency ~75% with minimal loss; NeMo Guardrails for programmable rails, maintained at NVIDIA-NeMo/Guardrails but cadence has slowed, latest release v0.23.0 (Jul 2025). Newer entrant: OpenAI's gpt-oss-safeguard (Oct 2025), open-weight classifiers that reason over a policy you supply at inference time, notable, not yet the standard.
Incident response playbook

(1) Containment: disable the feature or route, log the window of affected traffic; (2) Evidence: preserve raw inputs, model outputs, and full traces for the affected session IDs; (3) Scope: estimate how many users/transactions were affected; (4) Disclosure: legal/compliance determines notification obligations; (5) Remediation: patch the specific control that failed; (6) Post-mortem: add the attack to the red-team suite so it never silently recurs.
mistakes: Relying on prompt-based injection defense ('ignore instructions in retrieved content') as the primary control, it's a layer, not a gate
Red-teaming after launch instead of before, the first incident does the red-team for you
Assuming a specific jailbreak won't work because 'our model has strong alignment', all models break under sufficient pressure
Testing only direct injection, missing the indirect injection vectors through documents and tool results
Privileged tool calls (send, delete, pay) authorized by model-parsed content instead of server-side session state
No incident response playbook before the first security event, every action improvised under pressure
flags: "Our system prompt tells the model to ignore injection attempts", prompt-based security theater
"We haven't red-teamed yet, but we're launching next week"
"Tool results go straight into the context" without sanitization or untrusted-content framing
"The model won't do that", unvalidated assumption, zero empirical evidence
ask: What are every channel through which attacker-controlled content can reach the model context?
What happens if a document in our RAG index contains a well-crafted injection payload?
Which tool calls can the model trigger without human approval, and what's the worst-case blast radius?
When did we last run an automated red-team sweep, and what does the schedule look like?

MODULES.title: AI Observability & Production Reliability
MODULES.tag: Distributed tracing, quality SLOs, and drift detection: the instrumentation layer you build before the first incident
MODULES.why: AI systems fail silently. Wrong answers come back with 200 OK. Quality drifts over weeks while the dashboards stay green. Costs run away without ever tripping an error budget. Standard APM is necessary but nowhere near sufficient. Staff engineers design the observability architecture before the system ships, because retrofitting it after the first quality incident always costs more than building it in.
MODULES.mental: Treat the quality metric time series as the heartbeat of your AI system. Latency and error rate tell you whether the HTTP layer is healthy. They tell you nothing about whether the model is hallucinating at 12%. Every AI production system needs three instruments: traces (what did the model see and do), quality scores (is it doing it well), and drift alerts (is the distribution shifting). Miss any one, and you'll hear about it from users first.
concepts: Distributed tracing for agentic systems

Standard HTTP spans capture the network call. AI-specific span attributes (OpenTelemetry GenAI semantic conventions): gen_ai.system, gen_ai.request.model, gen_ai.usage.input_tokens, gen_ai.usage.output_tokens. Custom attributes for agent loops: cost_usd, tool_call_name, trajectory_id (shared across all turns in one agent session), loop_iteration. Every tool call is a child span; sub-agent invocations are linked traces. Without trajectory_id, debugging a multi-turn agent failure is archaeology.
SLOs for probabilistic systems

Latency SLOs (p50/p95/p99) work unchanged. Quality SLOs require a measurable metric: faithfulness_rate (from async online eval scoring), task_success_rate, abstention_rate. Define error budget as: X% of traffic allowed below the quality threshold per rolling week. The discipline of writing down 'we will alert if faithfulness_rate drops below 82% on a 7-day rolling window' forces you to define what quality means before shipping.
Online eval sampling pipelines

Sample 2–5% of production traffic into an async queue. Score each sample with a cheap judge model (different family from the generator). Write scores + trace IDs to a time-series store. Alert on rolling-average regression (7-day window, threshold drift > 3 points from 30-day baseline). This is the only instrument that catches quality degradation before users do.
Behavioral drift vs data distribution drift vs performance drift

Behavioral drift: model output distribution changed, detect via semantic embedding shift in sampled responses (KL divergence or drift distance on response embedding centroids). Data distribution drift: incoming query distribution shifted, detect via embedding shift in input queries. Performance drift: quality metric dropped, detect via online eval score series. These have different causes and different responses: performance drift is the alert to action; behavioral and data drift are the diagnosis.
Canary and shadow deployment for AI

Canary: route 5% of traffic to the new version, score both canary and control via async evals, auto-rollback if canary quality score drops more than N points vs control. The AI difference from standard software canaries: error rates alone won't catch a prompt regression that answers confidently but wrongly. Shadow: route 100% of traffic to both versions, compare quality scores offline without serving shadow responses. Use shadow for high-risk changes.
Incident playbooks for AI-specific failure modes

Hallucination spike: faithfulness_rate alert triggers, sample 50 affected traces, check if a model alias auto-upgraded or prompt changed, disable feature if rate > 2× baseline. Cost runaway: per-route budget alert, check output token growth and cache hit rate drop, identify the route. Prompt injection event: quarantine affected session IDs, identify what was served to whom, evidence preservation before remediation. Each playbook should exist before the incident, not be written during it.
AI-ready monitoring vs bolt-on APM

Standard APM: requests/errors/latency, necessary but not sufficient. AI-ready adds: (1) quality metric time series from async eval scoring; (2) per-route cost metrics (USD/request with alert thresholds); (3) semantic drift dashboards for inputs and outputs; (4) model version and prompt version tracking; (5) token utilization breakdown (input/output, cached/uncached). Langfuse, Arize Phoenix, and Braintrust all provide this; OpenTelemetry GenAI conventions let you build it yourself into any OTEL backend.
mistakes: Monitoring only latency and error rate, correct latency with wrong answers is undetected by both
SLOs defined exclusively on infrastructure metrics; quality SLOs not written down before launch
Detecting quality degradation from support tickets rather than from monitoring, users are a lagging, biased instrument
Canary deployments that check error rates without checking quality scores on canary vs control traffic
No trajectory IDs in traces, multi-turn agent failures can't be reconstructed from individual span logs
Retrofitting observability after the first quality incident, treating it as optional infrastructure
flags: "The dashboards look green" when only latency and error rate are on the dashboard
