"We found out from support tickets that quality dropped", no quality monitoring
"We can't trace what the agent did on that specific request", no trajectory IDs
"We deploy AI prompt changes the same way as API bug fixes", no quality canary
ask: What is the quality metric for this feature, and what value triggers an alert?
Can you pull a complete trace for any specific user interaction, including every model call and tool result?
What percentage of production traffic is scored asynchronously for quality, and how often?
What does the on-call playbook say to do when the faithfulness rate alert fires?

MODULES.title: Data Engineering for AI Systems
MODULES.tag: The pipeline that sets your retrieval ceiling: chunking, embedding lifecycle, and the data flywheel
MODULES.why: The model and the retrieval system are only as good as the data pipeline feeding them. Bad chunking, mixed embedding versions, stale ACLs, and missing re-indexing triggers quietly cap quality at 60–70% before you write a single prompt. Staff engineers design the data architecture so the retrieval system improves on its own over time, instead of needing a manual tune-up every quarter.
MODULES.mental: The data pipeline is the invisible quality ceiling. Every downstream optimization (better models, better prompts, better rerankers) operates on whatever your pipeline hands them. A table split across two chunks, a stale document served as current, or an embedding model mismatch produces plausible-looking garbage with no error signal. Design the pipeline as if retrieval quality is a function of pipeline correctness first and model quality second.
concepts: Document preprocessing pipelines

OCR quality gates: Tesseract fails on low-resolution, handwritten, and complex-layout scanned docs; commercial APIs (AWS Textract, Azure AI Document Intelligence, Reducto.ai) handle structured layouts but are expensive. Score OCR confidence per page and quarantine low-confidence pages for human review rather than silently ingesting garbage. Structure extraction: layout detection models (LayoutLMv3, Microsoft Table Transformer) to locate tables, headers, and figures before chunking. Normalization: Unicode normalization, header deduplication, whitespace and formatting artifact removal.
Chunking strategy design

Fixed-size (e.g. 512 tokens / 50-token overlap): fast, breaks semantic units, catastrophically fragments tables. Never use as the default. Semantic chunking: split at low-similarity sentence transitions (sentence-transformers to detect boundary points). Hierarchical: parent (section, ~1500 tokens) + child (paragraph, ~400 tokens); retrieve on child granularity, return parent for generation context, balances retrieval precision with generation context richness. Late chunking: embed the full document, pool sub-embeddings from full-context representations; preserves inter-chunk context ('the regulation described above') in the embedding itself.
Parent-child retrieval

Retrieve at child granularity (precise vector match), serve parent context to the model (full section with surrounding material). LlamaIndex ParentDocumentRetriever implements this. The concrete win: a 400-token child chunk retrieves with high precision; the 1500-token parent gives the model the surrounding context it needs to answer correctly. Without this, precision and recall trade off with a single chunk size.
Embedding pipeline reliability

Version the embedding model as a first-class artifact, store model ID + version in index metadata, raise a hard error on startup if the deployed embedder mismatches the index. Re-embedding triggers: model upgrade (always), significant format change, domain shift detected via recall regression. Blue-green migration: build the new index while the old one serves, run recall comparison on the golden query set, atomic alias swap. Never mix versions in the same index.
Data flywheel design

Production failures → labeling queue → eval cases → (eventually) training signal. Pipeline: failure detection (low faithfulness score, user thumbs-down, empty retrieval result) → automatic sampling into a labeling queue → human labeling with a rubric → permanent eval case added to the golden set → quarterly review for training signal. The flywheel means the system gets measurably better every week without a dedicated improvement sprint.
Synthetic data generation

Safe for: expanding eval coverage of rare but real query types; generating diverse phrasings of documented facts (backtranslation: answer → question generation). Creates false confidence when used for: training data on factual domains, the generator hallucinates facts into training examples. Adversarial filtering: generate a large pool, filter with a binary judge (factually grounded? diverse from existing set?), keep the top 20%. Never use raw model-generated synthetic data as training data without this filter.
Knowledge graph integration

Entity extraction (spaCy, custom NER) → graph construction (Neo4j, or in-process with networkx). Hybrid retrieval: vector for semantic similarity, graph for multi-hop relationships ('find the manager's direct reports' cannot be answered by cosine similarity alone). Entity disambiguation: 'Apple' in 'Apple vs Samsung' is AAPL; in 'apple allergy' it's the fruit, graphs store canonical entities and their context. Use graph traversal when queries require relationship chains that span multiple documents.
Data quality dimensions for RAG

Freshness: track last-modified timestamp per chunk; alert when chunks exceed the freshness SLA (e.g. >72 hours behind source). Access control propagation: when source document permissions change, the change must propagate to all derived chunks within a defined window, stale ACLs leak restricted content. Deduplication: SimHash or MinHash LSH at ingestion to avoid duplicate chunks boosting a single source's retrieval weight; deduplicate top-k results before reranking.
mistakes: Fixed-size chunking as the production default, splits tables, clauses, and numbered lists at arbitrary boundaries
No version tracking on the embedding model used to build each index, silent quality collapse on any dependency update
Tables ingested as raw text, losing row/column relationships entirely
No freshness tracking, stale documents served as current with no staleness signal to the model or user
Synthetic training data generated without adversarial filtering, hallucinations baked into training signal
ACL propagation not implemented, permissions change on the source, chunks remain accessible to unauthorized users
flags: "We chunk at 512 characters", arbitrary, format-blind, table-destroying
"We ingested all our documents at launch and re-ingest monthly"
"The embedding model is just a dependency in requirements.txt", not pinned as an artifact with index metadata
"Tables aren't really a problem for us", hasn't looked at what the pipeline actually produces for tables
ask: How are table structures preserved through the chunking pipeline? Show me a table from a real document post-chunking.
What triggers a document chunk to be re-indexed after the source document is updated?
How does the chunk's access control map to the source document's permissions, and what's the propagation latency?
What is the pipeline from a production retrieval failure to a permanent eval case?

MODULES.title: Multimodal Systems & Document Intelligence
MODULES.tag: Vision-language pipelines, document ingestion at scale, and when to pay for vision vs when to skip it
MODULES.why: Enterprise document workflows (insurance claims, legal filings, financial reports, technical manuals) are full of tables, figures, and scanned content that text-only pipelines handle badly. Building multimodal document intelligence that stays reliable at scale means knowing when vision adds real value, when it's expensive theater, and how to route by document type instead of treating everything the same.
MODULES.mental: Vision-language models are an expensive retrieval upgrade for content your text pipeline can't see. The question is never 'can the model handle images?' It can. The question is whether the value of what vision recovers (a table structure, a figure's data, handwritten annotations) justifies 10–50× the cost, plus the added latency, over text extraction. The same page priced on a $5/MTok frontier multimodal model (Claude Opus 5, GPT-5.6 Sol) instead of the $0.20/MTok text tier (GPT-5.6 Luna) is 25× on the model bill alone, and pdfminer extraction itself is free. For digital-native PDFs with clean text layers, the answer is almost always no. Route first, vision second.
concepts: Vision-language model selection in 2026

Claude Opus 5 / GPT-5.6 Sol class (both $5/MTok input): best for complex mixed-layout documents, structured data extraction from tables, figure understanding. Gemini 3.6 Flash ($1.50/$7.50 per MTok, 1M context): strong multimodal at 30% of the frontier input price; long-context advantage for multi-page documents. Open-weight: MiniMax M3 (June 2026, natively multimodal, 1M context) is the current pick for high-volume, cost-sensitive, or data-residency-bound workloads with a self-hosting budget; Llama 4 Vision is no longer frontier but is still the most-deployed open family with the widest tooling. The open VLM roster turns over every few months, re-check artificialanalysis.ai before committing. Cost profile: a single 1000×1000px page ≈ 800–1600 image tokens (model-dependent, verify against your provider's current vision docs), and those tokens get priced on a $5/MTok multimodal model instead of the $0.20/MTok tier that extracted text could have used, 10–50× the cost of text extraction on digital-native PDFs.
PDF and document ingestion pipeline design

Digital-native PDFs: pdfminer.six or pypdf for text extraction, fast, free, accurate. Never send these to a vision model. Scanned PDFs: AWS Textract, Azure AI Document Intelligence, or Google Document AI for production; Tesseract for low-budget. Score OCR confidence per page; quarantine pages below 0.7 confidence for human review. Layout detection: LayoutLMv3 or Detectron2-based models to locate tables, headers, figures before extracting. Table extraction: Microsoft Table Transformer (TATR), locate table regions, then extract structure with row/column relationships preserved. Camelot (rule-based) works only on digital-native, fails on scanned.
Audio input patterns

Transcribe first (Whisper large-v3, ~$0.006/min, WER 2–4% on clear audio): enables all text-side processing, chunking, retrieval, structured extraction. Best for most use cases. Pass raw audio to multimodal model: necessary when the task requires speaker identity (diarization, pyannote-audio), prosodic cues (emotion, emphasis, hesitation), or acoustic environment analysis. Cost: raw audio calls to frontier models are significantly more expensive than transcription + text call. The routing decision: does the task require audio-native signals, or just what was said?
Structured data as context

NL2SQL: include the relevant table schemas (not all 500 tables) in context alongside the user question; retrieve relevant tables first via schema embedding similarity. For large databases (>50 tables), schema filtering is mandatory, attention can't find the right JOIN across 500 schemas. CSV in context: tables under ~150 rows can be included directly; larger tables need code execution (pandas) or NL2SQL. Schema-in-context tradeoffs: full schema enables flexible queries but consumes context budget; filtered schema is cheaper but may miss needed tables.
Cross-modal eval design

End-to-end task accuracy is insufficient, it hides which modality failed. Separate metrics: (1) OCR accuracy: character error rate on a held-out set of scanned documents; (2) Table extraction precision: % of cells correctly extracted with correct row/column assignment; (3) Figure understanding accuracy: key data points correctly identified from charts; (4) Answer faithfulness: standard RAG faithfulness metric on the final answers. Component metrics localize failures; end-to-end tells the user's truth.
When multimodal beats text-only

Complex tables where structure is visual (spanning cells, nested headers), text extraction loses relationships. Figures and charts where the data is not present in the surrounding text. Handwritten annotations. Scanned documents where OCR quality is insufficient for precise extraction but a VLM can tolerate some noise. Mixed-layout documents where column detection matters (newspapers, product catalogs). Multimodal is NOT better for: digital-native PDFs with clean text, simple tabular data where Camelot works, any document where pdfminer extracts clean structured text.
Latency and cost profile of vision calls

A 50-page PDF at 1000×1000px per page: ~50K image tokens on a frontier multimodal model (Claude Opus 5 or GPT-5.6 Sol, $5/MTok input) = $0.25 per document, $0.50 on Claude Fable 5 at $10/MTok. The same 50 pages through pdfminer costs CPU and no API spend, and the ~50K tokens of extracted text run on the $0.20/MTok tier (GPT-5.6 Luna) for $0.01. Same content, 25–50× the bill, because page images are usually pinned to the frontier multimodal tier while extracted text is not. Short-circuit logic: detect if a PDF has a text layer (pdfminer returns non-empty text) → use text pipeline; no text layer → route to vision. Cache document analyses aggressively: if the same document is processed repeatedly (common in enterprise), extract once, cache the structured output, skip all future vision calls for that document version.
mistakes: Running vision model calls on digital-native PDFs with extractable text, 10–50× cost overhead for no quality improvement
Not scoring OCR confidence and serving low-confidence extractions as ground truth
Using fixed-size chunking on tables, produces cell fragments the model can't interpret
Including the full database schema in NL2SQL context for a 200-table database
No separate evaluation metrics for table, figure, and text modalities, end-to-end accuracy hides which component is failing
No caching for processed documents in high-volume pipelines, vision calls run on every request
flags: "We use vision on all our PDFs", no short-circuit for digital-native documents
"OCR quality is fine" without any measured character error rate
"We include the whole database schema" for NL2SQL
"We can't evaluate figure understanding", that means the pipeline is untested on its hardest cases
ask: What fraction of documents are digital-native vs scanned, and how does the pipeline route between them?
What is our measured OCR character error rate on a sample of real production documents?
How do we handle a document whose critical data is only in figures, not in the surrounding text?
What is the end-to-end latency and cost for processing a 100-page PDF, broken down by stage?

llm.q: A chatbot's monthly bill doubled while traffic stayed flat. Two weeks ago the team shipped 'more detailed answers.' Which lever do you investigate FIRST?
o: Input token growth as longer conversation histories accumulate and re-send on every turn
A prompt cache hit-rate regression triggered by the new prompt invalidating the cached prefix
Output tokens per response, detail means longer completions at 3–5× input price
A quiet provider price increase on the model tier you're running, applied without notice
llm.exp: All four can move a bill, but the timing points at the change: 'more detail' = longer outputs, and output is both the priciest token class and the latency driver. History growth (A) and cache regression (B) are real effects worth checking second, but they don't double a bill in two weeks the way doubled completion length does.

llm.q: With temperature=0, a team gets slightly different outputs on identical requests and files it as a provider bug. The accurate assessment?
o: It's a genuine bug, greedy decoding is deterministic by definition, so any drift proves the stack is misconfigured somewhere
Expected: providers don't guarantee bitwise reproducibility (batching, hardware variance); enforce determinism at the application layer
You also need top_p=0 and a fixed seed, since temperature=0 alone only partially reduces sampling randomness
The drift comes from prompt cache hits returning slightly stale completions across otherwise identical calls
llm.exp: Greedy decoding is deterministic in theory (A's logic), but real serving stacks batch requests and vary across hardware, so providers explicitly don't guarantee reproducibility. Seeds (C) help on some APIs but still carry no guarantee. If you need determinism, build it yourself: cache by input hash, canonicalize outputs.

llm.q: On your eval, a Haiku-class model scores within 1% of the flagship for a classification route. An engineer argues for the flagship anyway: 'headroom for harder future cases.' Strongest counter?
o: Agree, but negotiate a volume discount on the flagship to make the headroom argument cheaper to honor
Run both in production 50/50 for a quarter and let live quality metrics settle the disagreement
Fine-tune the small model first to close the remaining 1% gap, then revisit the tiering decision
Route to the small model now; add an escalation path for the hard slice when it actually appears
llm.exp: 'Headroom' is paying 10–12× today for cases that don't exist yet. Tier-and-escalate gets you the savings now and a designed path for hard cases later. The 50/50 test (B) burns half the savings to learn what the eval already told you; fine-tuning (C) adds work before capturing free wins.

llm.q: Your request has a 5K-token static block (system prompt + tool definitions) and ~1K of per-request data. Which layout maximizes prompt-cache savings?
o: Static block first and byte-stable; per-request data appended last
Per-request data first so it's freshest, with the static block placed after it
Interleave static and dynamic sections so partial segments still cache-match
Static block moved into the first user message, with the system kept minimal
llm.exp: Caching matches the leading prefix byte-for-byte: stable-first layouts cache the 5K block (up to 90% off); any volatile content before it, or one edited byte inside it, invalidates everything after. B optimizes for an attention concern that placement at the end already serves (recency).

llm.q: A colleague claims 1M-token windows have made RAG obsolete: 'just send everything.' The strongest technical counter is:
o: Models can't actually attend past ~200K tokens regardless of the advertised window size, so the larger numbers are pure marketing spec-sheet padding
Filling 1M tokens costs $0.14–$10 per call, adds serious latency, degrades mid-window recall, and bypasses per-user access control
Long-context windows will be deprecated soon as providers shift to retrieval-native model architectures anyway
RAG remains strictly cheaper to build and operate than long-context prompting at essentially any workload scale
llm.exp: B stacks the four real arguments: per-call economics, latency, lost-in-the-middle (reduced, not solved), and ACL enforcement, which requires retrieval-time filtering. A overstates (long-window recall is degraded, not zero); C is invented; D is false in general, RAG pipelines carry real engineering cost.

prompt.q: A teammate improved a support prompt's tone Friday; by Monday, refund-eligibility answers (same prompt) regressed 12%. The ROOT failure to fix is:
o: No regression gate: a multi-behavior prompt changed without an eval suite covering all its behaviors
No version pinning: an older prompt variant shipped alongside the new one and served some traffic
Tone and policy instructions inherently conflict, so they have to live in two separate models
No human QA: the change should have run against 50 real transcripts before it reached production
prompt.exp: The systemic fix is treating prompts as code: eval coverage spanning every behavior the prompt serves, gating every change. Manual QA (D) is a weaker, non-repeating version of the same idea. Pinning (B) addresses a different failure class. C overreacts, separation of concerns means decomposed prompts, not separate models.

prompt.q: You need machine-parseable JSON from a model on every call. The production-grade approach is:
o: Few-shot prompting with five well-chosen JSON examples that cover the known edge cases
Temperature 0 plus an explicit 'respond ONLY with valid JSON' instruction in the system prompt
Schema-enforced structured output, so invalid JSON is unsamplable by construction
A tolerant parser with automatic repair logic and a single retry whenever parsing fails
prompt.exp: Constrained decoding masks invalid tokens during generation, the failure class is removed, not reduced. Few-shot (A) and instructions (B) lower the error rate; repair-and-retry (D) is a reasonable backstop but as the primary strategy it means owning a parser and a tail of weird failures forever.

prompt.q: A model keeps using bullet points despite 'Do NOT use bullet points' in the system prompt. The highest-yield fix:
o: Repeat the prohibition at both the start and the end of the system prompt for emphasis
Add a frequency penalty during decoding to suppress the list-marker tokens it keeps emitting
Move the rule into the user turn instead, where it sits closest to the point of generation
Rephrase positively with a short example of the desired prose format the model should follow
prompt.exp: Models follow 'do X, like this' far better than 'don't do Y', prohibitions name the wrong thing without showing the right one. Repetition (A) and placement (C) buy marginal gains; decoding penalties (B) are a blunt instrument that damages legitimate text.

prompt.q: You're moving a hard analytical task to a native reasoning model. Your old prompt has elaborate 'think step-by-step: first…, then…, finally…' scaffolding. You should:
o: Keep the scaffolding, since explicit step-by-step structure can only help a reasoning model arrive at a more reliable answer
Strip it: state the task and quality bar plainly; the model reasons internally and double-scaffolding can degrade output
Keep it, but relocate it into a dedicated scratchpad field the model fills in before it answers
Convert the scaffold into a few-shot example showing a full worked reasoning chain end to end
prompt.exp: Reasoning models internalized chain-of-thought during training; imposed scaffolds waste tokens and can fight the model's own decomposition. A and C feel safe but micromanage; D pays example-tokens on every call for reasoning the model already does. Spend the effort on task clarity and output contracts.

prompt.q: Which observation most strongly indicates a prompt is doing too many jobs?
o: It exceeds 2,000 tokens and packs both detailed instructions and several few-shot examples together
It depends on both a system section and per-request user content in order to produce a result
Editing it for one intent keeps regressing unrelated intents that happen to share the same prompt
It relies on XML tags to delimit more than five visually distinct sections within the prompt body
prompt.exp: Coupling under change is the tell, same as a god-class in code. Length (A), structure (B), and sectioning (D) are all compatible with a well-scoped prompt; non-local regressions are not. The fix is decomposition: a router plus focused prompts, each separately evaluable.

context.q: An agent's output quality degrades noticeably around turn 40, yet the context window is only half full. Most likely cause?
o: Provider-side KV-cache eviction kicking in once a long-running session passes a hidden duration limit
Positional encoding quality degrading sharply once turns push past the model's original training length
Context rot: accumulated stale tool output, dead ends, and repetition conditioning the model toward noise
The system prompt's steering influence decaying steadily as each new turn grows its distance from it
context.exp: The window isn't full, it's polluted. Models are pattern completers, and 40 turns of unpruned tool dumps and abandoned reasoning actively condition worse output. A and B sound mechanical but don't apply at half-capacity; D has a grain of truth (recency effects) but isn't the dominant failure here. Prune and compact.

context.q: Critical compliance rules sit at ~token 60K of a 120K prompt and get intermittently ignored. The mechanism at fault:
o: Lost-in-the-middle: attention is strongest at the start and end of context; mid-window content gets the weakest coverage
The rules blew past the model's instruction-following budget, which tops out around a few dozen directives
The rules sit in the user turn, but compliance content has to be in the system role to bind reliably
120K tokens exceeds the model's reliable attention span, so the call needs to be split into two passes
context.exp: Position, not count or role, is the failure: U-shaped attention is a well-documented empirical property. Move non-negotiables to the start, keep the live question at the end. B's 'instruction budget' isn't the binding constraint here; C matters but doesn't explain position-dependent failures; D gives up a workable window.

context.q: Your agent occasionally needs content from a 300-page manual. The best context strategy:
o: Embed the full manual in the system prompt once and lean on prompt caching to keep each call cheap
Maintain a hand-built 2-page summary of the manual and include it in every single request you send
Give the agent search/read tools to fetch relevant sections just-in-time
Fine-tune the model directly on the manual so the content lives in weights and needs no context at all
context.exp: JIT retrieval keeps the window clean and adapts to what each task needs. Caching (A) softens cost but not the accuracy hit of a stuffed window, and 'occasionally needs' means most calls pay for nothing. The summary (B) loses exactly the detail that makes a manual useful; fine-tuning (D) is slow, expensive, and bad at verbatim recall.

context.q: A long-running agent relies on compaction summaries to carry key decisions across sessions, and decisions keep getting lost. The durable fix:
o: Raise the compaction threshold so that many more raw turns survive fully untouched before each summarization pass is finally allowed to run
Persist critical decisions to durable artifacts (progress files, structured notes) that each session reads at boot
Run compaction more frequently so every individual summary covers less and therefore loses less
Pin each decision into the system prompt the moment it's made so it can never be summarized away
context.exp: Compaction is lossy by design, tuning its frequency (A, C) just moves which information dies. The harness lesson: state that must survive lives outside the context, in files/git the next session reads. Pinning to the system prompt (D) works briefly, then becomes its own unbounded context problem.

context.q: Why spawn a sub-agent for a broad codebase search rather than running it in the main loop?
o: A sub-agent can run on a cheaper model, which cuts the raw cost of doing the broad search itself
Several parallel sub-agents return their results faster than one sequential in-loop search would
Tool-output size limits in the main loop would otherwise truncate the broad search's raw results
A fresh-context sub-agent absorbs the noisy intermediate output and returns only the conclusion
context.exp: The point is context hygiene: broad searches dump thousands of noisy tokens that would rot the main window for the rest of the session. Cheaper models (A) and parallelism (B) are nice side benefits, not the reason; C describes a symptom you'd work around, not the design rationale.

landscape.q: A team argues they no longer need to benchmark new model releases because 'the frontier models are all basically the same now, 1M+ context, similar quality.' The strongest technical rebuttal:
o: Leaderboards still show 10–15 point gaps between frontier models on hard reasoning tasks, and the gaps widen further on long-horizon agentic benchmarks, so they are plainly not all the same caliber
1M+ windows are commoditized, but 71× cost spreads to fill the same window make context volume a first-class routing decision, and harness quality swamps model deltas on agentic tasks
Benchmark contamination makes frontier scores unreliable, so any apparent similarity between models could just reflect memorized public test sets
Open-weight models have now closed the gap so far that which closed frontier model you happen to pick barely matters for real-world quality
landscape.exp: The cost-spread argument (71× from cheapest to most expensive per 1M tokens) is the practical rebuttal to 'they're all the same', same window size does not mean same economics. And the harness-sensitivity data (same model scoring 36 points apart under different scaffolding) means that for agentic work, model choice is often the second-order variable anyway. A means baseline differences still exist. C and D are real but softer points that do not address the team's actual argument.

landscape.q: Filling the same 1M-token window costs $0.14 on one frontier model and ~$10 on another. The correct architectural takeaway:
o: Standardize on the single cheapest 1M model so that long context becomes affordable everywhere by default
Context volume is a first-class cost decision: tier and route by task instead of defaulting to one model
Cap every production context at 128K tokens until per-token prices across the frontier finally converge
Treat the premium models as mispriced and assume the 71× spread will mostly close within a single quarter
landscape.exp: A 71× spread is a routing signal, not a verdict on any single model: cheap tiers for high-volume easy work, premium for the hard slice. Standardizing on the cheapest (A) ignores quality differences; blanket caps (C) solve cost by capping capability; price-convergence bets (D) are hope, not architecture.

landscape.q: A team selected its production model because it tops a public leaderboard. The most substantive senior-level objection:
o: Public leaderboards lag actual model releases by several months, so the headline ranking you chose from is already stale by the time you ship
Arena-style rankings overweight chat style and formatting polish over genuine correctness on real tasks
Public benchmarks are contaminated; the top models have effectively memorized the published test sets
Leaderboard deltas compress on your real traffic, and on agentic tasks harness quality swamps model deltas, validate on your own evals
landscape.exp: B and C name real, partial issues, style bias and contamination exist, but the decision-grade objection is D: your distribution isn't the benchmark's, the deltas shrink on the easy middle of real traffic, and the published 78/42 same-model result shows scaffolding can outweigh model choice entirely.

landscape.q: What actually makes model-switching cost approach zero?
o: Restricting all usage to OpenAI-compatible API surfaces so that any provider can be dropped in unchanged
A gateway abstraction plus versioned prompts plus a standing eval suite to validate the swap
Avoiding every provider-specific feature (caching, tool use, structured output) from day one for portability
Negotiating multi-vendor contracts up front with explicit capability-parity clauses across the providers
landscape.exp: Wire compatibility (A) gets requests flowing but says nothing about behavior, the eval suite is what tells you the swap is safe, and the gateway makes it a config change. Avoiding provider features (C) buys portability by forfeiting the platform's best capabilities; contracts (D) don't move code.

landscape.q: Open-weight models (DeepSeek V4, Qwen 3.6, MiniMax M3) earn a place in your stack when:
o: You need the absolute best quality on hard multi-step reasoning, where every last point of accuracy matters
Sub-100ms latency requirements rule out hosted API round-trips, forcing inference onto your own boxes
High-volume cost-sensitive or data-residency-bound workloads justify funding real self-hosting MLOps
Your security team enforces a blanket policy against sending any data to third-party APIs, full stop
landscape.exp: The honest case is unit economics at volume and hard residency requirements, bought with real serving infrastructure and on-call. A is still the closed frontier's edge; B is solvable with hosted regional endpoints; D describes a constraint that forces the choice rather than a case where it earns it (and enterprise API tiers usually satisfy security teams).

rag.q: RAG answers are mediocre and the team is on its third generation-prompt rewrite. What do you check FIRST?
o: Run a faithfulness eval to see whether the generation step is contradicting the passages it was actually given
Raise top-k so more candidate passages reach the model, on the theory that more context lifts answer quality
Measure retrieval recall@k on a golden set, is the right passage even being retrieved before the model sees it?
Swap to the newest embedding model and rebuild the index, assuming better vectors will surface better passages
rag.exp: Retrieval ceiling-caps the system: if the right chunk isn't in context, no prompt fixes it, and typical unmeasured pipelines miss 30–50% of the time. Faithfulness checks (A) come after you know the inputs are good; raising k (B) and re-embedding (D) are changes made blind without the recall number.

rag.q: Users searching exact part numbers ('XR-4421') get irrelevant results from a vector-only pipeline. The targeted fix:
o: Add BM25/keyword search fused with the dense results, exact identifiers are lexical search's home turf
Increase chunk overlap at ingestion so part numbers never get split across a chunk boundary and lost
Fine-tune the embedding model on your part-number vocabulary so identifiers embed into distinct neighborhoods
Normalize identifiers into a single canonical form at both ingestion and query time so the strings line up
rag.exp: Dense vectors blur exact strings by design; hybrid retrieval is the standard fix. B addresses a different failure (split chunks); C can help eventually but is weeks of work for what fusion fixes today; D helps matching consistency but doesn't make a semantic index respect exact tokens.

rag.q: A pipeline feeds raw top-10 vector hits straight into the prompt. The cheapest upgrade with the largest precision gain:
o: Decompose each query into sub-queries and retrieve for every one of them in parallel, then merge the hits
Apply HyDE-style query expansion before retrieval so a hypothetical answer pulls in closer-matching passages
Raise top-k to 30 and rely on the model to read past the irrelevant passages and answer from the good ones
Run a cross-encoder reranker over the top 50–100 candidates and keep only the best 5–10 for the prompt
rag.exp: Reranking is the classic underused stage: one component, ~100ms, large precision win, the cross-encoder's joint attention re-scores what the coarse bi-encoder fetched. Query decomposition (A) and HyDE (B) are real but heavier techniques; raising k without reranking (C) imports noise and pays for it twice.

rag.q: Your RAG assistant answers questions about documents the asking user has no permission to open. The correct fix:
o: Add an output filter that redacts content sourced from restricted documents before it is shown to the user
Enforce document ACLs inside the retrieval query so restricted chunks never reach the context in the first place
Instruct the model in the system prompt to check each source's permissions before using it in an answer
Maintain separate indexes per sensitivity tier and route each query to one based on the user's clearance level
rag.exp: Authorization belongs in the retrieval layer, filter by the requesting user's permissions at query time. Output redaction (A) means the leak already happened in-context; prompt-level checks (C) make the model a security boundary, which it isn't; per-tier indexes (D) can work but is a heavyweight redesign of what a query filter solves.

rag.q: What distinguishes agentic RAG (the 2026 pattern) from a classic pipeline?
o: Retrieved passages are checked by a separate judge model for relevance before they are allowed into the context
Queries are decomposed offline by a planner model into a fixed retrieval plan that runs the same way every time
Multiple specialized indexes are always queried together in parallel and their results fused into one ranked list
The model treats search as a tool, deciding when and what to query, evaluating the results, and iterating as needed
rag.exp: The defining shift is retrieval moving into the loop under the model's control, adaptive, multi-query, self-evaluating. A describes a guardrail you can add to either pattern; B is still a fixed pre-step (the opposite of adaptive); C describes federation, which is orthogonal.

rag.q: Your RAG pipeline shows recall@10 = 69% on a golden set but recall@50 = 94%. An engineer proposes sending all 50 chunks to the model. The correct response:
o: Approve it, 94% recall is a big jump and feeding all 50 chunks should directly raise the answer quality here
Acceptable for short documents where the 50 chunks fit the context window comfortably without crowding it out
Reject: context pollution degrades generation; add a cross-encoder reranker to keep the best 5–8 of the top 50
Approve it, but first add a diversity filter to drop the near-identical chunks so the 50 carry less redundancy
rag.exp: recall@50 = 94% confirms the relevant chunk is in the index, the bottleneck is ranking, not coverage. Passing 50 raw chunks pollutes the context window and pays token costs for noise. A reranker extracts signal and passes only what the model needs, this is precisely the gap the reranker stage exists to fill. A and D accept the wrong fix; B trades one scaling problem for a different one.

rag.q: Users query with internal abbreviations ('OOO policy', 'PTO reqs') but your HR document corpus consistently uses expanded phrases ('out-of-office policy', 'paid time off requirements'). Results from a semantic-only pipeline are poor. The cheapest targeted fix:
o: Fine-tune the embedding model on internal HR vocabulary so abbreviations embed near their expanded forms
Rewrite the user query to expand abbreviations before embedding, a single cheap LLM call at query time
Add BM25 to the hybrid stack on the theory that abbreviations are lexical patterns BM25 handles natively
Maintain a separate keyword index for short queries under 5 tokens, where most abbreviations tend to appear
rag.exp: Query expansion is the targeted fix: a cheap LLM call rewrites 'OOO policy' to 'out-of-office policy' before embedding, so the query lands in the same vector neighborhood as the corpus. BM25 (C) doesn't help here because the corpus uses the expanded form, 'OOO' and 'out-of-office' are different strings in both lexical and dense spaces; BM25 excels at exact token matches, not abbreviation-to-expansion bridging. Fine-tuning the embedder (A) teaches the model the vocabulary eventually, but it's weeks of work for a problem a one-line rewrite prompt solves today. A separate keyword index (D) has the same limitation as BM25, the abbreviation still doesn't match the expanded term. The diagnosis here is semantic drift from vocabulary mismatch, and expansion fixes it at the source.

rag.q: An append-only RAG index has been running 18 months. When policies update, new chunks are added but old ones are never deleted. Retrieval precision dropped from 61% to 44%. The most likely cause:
o: The embedding model's representation quality degrades as the corpus grows past a certain scale, weakening matches
ANN index fragmentation from continuous appends reduces recall, especially on the oldest entries in the graph
Semantic dilution: updated content coexists with its stale version, splitting retrieval votes between them
Top-k was quietly reduced during a cost-cutting sprint, so fewer relevant chunks now make it into each result
rag.exp: Append-only indexes accumulate semantic pollution: when a policy changes, old chunks stay and new ones are added, retrieval now surfaces both versions without knowing which is current. At 18 months, version coexistence dominates the precision loss. Index maintenance, staleness pruning, version supersession, deduplication, is the structural fix. ANN tuning and model swaps can't remedy data-layer contamination.

rag.q: Your RAG chatbot answers 'What is our standard refund policy?' correctly 93% of the time but 'What is the refund policy for international orders during a promotional sale?' only 38% of the time. The most likely structural cause:
o: The embedding model cannot reliably represent a query that combines several distinct concepts in one vector at once
The complete answer spans multiple sections, no single chunk holds the full intersection, so top-k returns fragments
The reranker is systematically down-weighting any chunk that happens to mention promotional or sale-related terminology
top-k is set too low to cover these compound queries, so the extra conditions push relevant chunks out of the results
rag.exp: Simple queries resolve against one chunk; compound queries require content spread across multiple chunks that rarely co-retrieve together in top-k. The fix is multi-query decomposition (retrieve separately for 'international refund' and 'promotional sale refund' then merge) or parent-document chunking that provides broader co-text. Neither the reranker nor top-k setting explains the specificity of this failure pattern.

rag.q: A RAG eval shows: when recall@5 succeeds (71% of queries), generation faithfulness is 84%. When retrieval fails, faithfulness drops to 28% as the model hallucinates into gaps. What is the effective faithful answer rate across ALL queries?
o: ~84%, since that's the faithfulness number on successful-retrieval queries
~68%, weighting faithfulness by the retrieval success and failure rates
~71%, since the faithful answer rate just tracks the retrieval recall rate
~78%, splitting the difference between the high and low faithfulness rates
rag.exp: Weight by retrieval outcome: (0.71 × 0.84) + (0.29 × 0.28) = 0.60 + 0.08 ≈ 68%. Reporting faithfulness only on successful-retrieval queries (A) ignores 29% of real traffic where the model fills gaps with hallucination, the most dangerous category. Retrieval recall and generation faithfulness are compounding failure modes, which is why you must measure both components separately to diagnose the system.

embed.q: After a routine embedding-model upgrade, search quality quietly collapsed, no errors anywhere. The cause:
o: The new model emits a different dimension count and the index silently truncated the extra values
The two models follow different vector-normalization conventions, quietly skewing every cosine score the ranker computes
Queries now embed in the new model's space while the corpus sits in the old one, cross-model similarity is meaningless
The new model expects input_type hints (query vs document) that the existing pipeline never sends
embed.exp: Two models' vector spaces have unrelated bases; comparing across them produces plausible-looking nonsense with zero errors. A would typically throw a dimension-mismatch error rather than degrade silently; B and D cause milder degradation, not collapse. Re-embed the corpus or roll back the query side.

embed.q: You must cut vector storage cost ~4× with minimal, measured quality loss. The modern first move:
o: Deduplicate near-identical chunks before embedding so the corpus, and its vector count, shrinks
Move the vectors for cold, rarely-touched documents over to keyword-only search to drop their storage
Re-embed the whole corpus with a smaller model that outputs fewer dimensions per vector to save space
Truncate Matryoshka dimensions or quantize, validating recall at each step
embed.exp: Matryoshka truncation and quantization are designed for exactly this, graceful, measurable degradation without re-embedding or model risk. Dedup (A) helps but rarely 4×; tiering to keyword (B) changes retrieval behavior for those docs; a smaller model (C) is a full migration with unknown quality, not a tuning knob.

embed.q: Legal-domain retrieval underperforms despite using a top-5 MTEB embedding model. The highest-leverage fix:
o: Chunk by the legal document's own structure (sections, clauses) instead of generic fixed-size boundaries
Fine-tune the embedding model on a few thousand in-domain query–passage pairs
Add a legal-domain reranker on top to compensate for misses coming out of first-stage retrieval
Expand each query with legal synonyms and citation forms at retrieval time to widen the match set
embed.exp: All four are real techniques, that's the trap. But MTEB rank ≠ jargon-heavy domain performance, and embedding fine-tuning attacks the root cause (the model's representation of legal language) for the largest recall gains. Structural chunking (A), reranking (C), and expansion (D) layer well on top, but they compensate rather than fix.

embed.q: Why do input_type hints (query vs document) measurably improve retrieval?
o: They route short queries to a smaller, faster encoder that's tuned specifically for brief text inputs
They normalize text length before pooling so that very short queries aren't unfairly penalized in scoring
Queries and documents are asymmetric text types; hinted models encode each appropriately
They make vectors from different model versions compatible, so old and new embeddings can be compared
embed.exp: A five-word question and a 500-word passage are different distributions; models trained with the distinction encode them into better-aligned spaces. A and B invent mechanisms; D is false, nothing bridges cross-model spaces.

embed.q: Beyond retrieval, which is a production-proven embedding application?
o: Lossless compression of long contexts into vectors before sending them on to the model to save tokens
Semantic caching: recognizing a new request as a paraphrase of an answered one and skipping the LLM call
Replacing cross-encoder rerankers outright at the same precision while costing meaningfully less to run
Encrypting stored documents in a form that still preserves the ability to search them semantically
embed.exp: Semantic cache is a workhorse cost lever on repetitive traffic. A is impossible (embeddings are lossy by definition); C inverts the architecture, bi-encoders are the coarse stage, cross-encoders the precise one; D describes searchable encryption, a different field entirely.

vecdb.q: A startup with 300K vectors already runs Postgres. The team wants a dedicated managed vector DB 'for growth headroom.' Your call:
o: Approve the managed DB, migrating later at 10M vectors will be far more painful than just starting on it now
Move to OpenSearch, since their logs already live there and it does vector search alongside the text it indexes
pgvector with HNSW, at this scale it removes a system while keeping joins, transactions, and ACLs
Run embedded FAISS inside the app with nightly snapshots, keeping the whole search path simple and in-process
vecdb.exp: Below ~5–10M vectors, the bolt-on wins on operational simplicity, and 'growth headroom' is speculative complexity, migration later is a real but bounded cost, paid only if growth materializes. OpenSearch (B) is plausible if it's already core infra, but adds an index tier they don't need; FAISS (D) trades durability and ops maturity for less than pgvector offers.

vecdb.q: ANN search with a selective tenant filter sometimes returns zero results although matches exist. The classic cause:
o: ef_search is set too low relative to the filter's selectivity, so raise it until the matching results appear
The engine post-filters: it fetches the top-k first, then applies the filter, which can eliminate all k
Tombstoned vectors from prior deletes are still being excluded, quietly shrinking the candidate set below k
The metadata index has drifted out of sync with the vector segments, so filter values no longer line up
vecdb.exp: Post-filtering is the textbook failure: selective filters annihilate an unfiltered top-k. A is the seductive wrong answer, raising ef_search papers over the architecture problem expensively and incompletely; the fix is pre-filter/filtered-ANN semantics. C and D are real operational issues with different signatures (gradual, not filter-correlated).

vecdb.q: Nobody has ever measured the ANN index's recall against exact search. The risk you're carrying:
o: Minimal risk, modern HNSW defaults reliably hold above 99% recall across essentially any production workload
Recall only becomes a concern above ~100M vectors, where the graph starts to fragment and lose neighbors
Silent relevance loss: speed-tuned parameters can quietly cap recall at 70–80%, bounding the whole RAG stack
No risk that matters, the downstream reranker recovers anything the index happens to miss before scoring it
vecdb.exp: ANN trades recall for speed by design, and tuning drift is silent, no errors, just worse answers. A's '>99% always' is exactly the assumption that bites; D misunderstands the pipeline: a reranker can only re-order what retrieval surfaced. Measure against brute force on a sample, monthly.

vecdb.q: Why should the vector index NOT serve as your source of truth?
o: Vector databases universally lack ACID guarantees, which makes them fundamentally unsafe to hold any system of record
Embeddings cannot be inverted back into their source text, so once you've stored only vectors the original data is unrecoverable
Storage and retention costs grow quadratically with corpus size in graph indexes, so keeping truth there gets far too expensive
It's a rebuildable derivative: embeddings change with model versions and ANN structures need rebuilds, truth belongs upstream
vecdb.exp: The index is disposable infrastructure with a rebuild path from a durable store, that's the architecture, regardless of any engine's ACID story (A is an overgeneralization; some offer strong guarantees). B is true but irrelevant if you store source text; C is invented.

vecdb.q: A tenant reports seeing another tenant's content in vector search results. The most likely design flaw:
o: Isolation relied on a soft metadata filter (or prompt instruction) instead of enforced namespaces/partitions at the index layer
Embedding collisions, where semantically similar content across two tenants maps to nearly identical vectors and then co-retrieves
A shared semantic cache is handing back another tenant's previously cached answer when two queries look close enough to match
HNSW graph edges are crossing tenant boundaries during traversal, letting one search wander into the wrong tenant's partition
vecdb.exp: Filters-by-convention fail exactly once and it's an incident; isolation must be enforced where the query executes. B describes normal embedding behavior, not leakage; C is a real adjacent risk but the report says search results; D anthropomorphizes the graph, traversal respects whatever isolation you actually enforced, which is the point.

memory.q: 'Our agent's memory is the last 50 messages.' The senior critique:
o: Fifty messages is too few, real personalization needs at least a few hundred turns of history to work from
That's working history, not memory: nothing is extracted, persisted, or selectively retrieved across sessions
Raw messages should be summarized before they're stored, otherwise the buffer wastes tokens carrying noise
The buffer should be bounded by token count rather than message count, so its context cost stays predictable
memory.exp: A buffer evaporates when the session ends and bloats context while it lives. Memory means extracted durable facts with provenance, retrieved selectively. A, C, and D all accept the buffer-as-memory premise and tune it, the premise is the error.

memory.q: A user corrected their dietary preference months ago; the assistant still serves the old one. Both facts are in the memory store. The ROOT design flaw:
o: Retrieval is ranking the older memory above the newer one, so adding recency boosting at read time would fix it
The extraction step failed to register how significant the correction was, so a stronger extractor model is needed
Append-only memory: contradictions must supersede prior facts at write time, not coexist
Preference-class memories carry no TTL, so stale facts persist indefinitely instead of expiring on their own
memory.exp: A and D are patches that leave the contradiction in the store, read-time recency (A) is fragile and TTLs (D) expire true facts too. The principled fix is at write: detect contradiction, supersede with history preserved. C (better extractor) misdiagnoses, the correction WAS captured; both facts exist.

memory.q: Why did file-based memory (progress files, MEMORY.md) win for long-running agents in 2026 harnesses?
o: Files let you avoid the embedding and vector-store costs that a semantic memory layer would otherwise add
Filesystem reads are faster than database reads from inside the agent sandbox, so lookups stay low-latency
Git history of the files doubles as provenance, making a separate provenance-tracking system unnecessary
Artifacts are durable, inspectable, survive compaction and crashes, and any session or harness can read them
memory.exp: The killer property is bridging amnesia: durable, human-auditable state that the next context window boots from. Cost (A) and speed (B) are incidental; git-as-provenance (C) is a genuine bonus but a side effect of the design, not the reason for it.

memory.q: The agent's memory contains 'user authorized purchases up to $500', extracted from a session where the user READ A PHISHING EMAIL ALOUD to ask if it was a scam. Weeks later the agent auto-approves a purchase. The core failure:
o: The extraction model was too small to grasp the conversational nuance, and a larger one would have prevented this whole thing
Authorization-class memories should require an exact-phrase match at retrieval time before they are ever allowed to be acted on
Memory poisoning: no provenance/speech-act check at write (quoted ≠ asserted), and memory content was trusted as instruction at read
The purchase tool was missing a per-transaction amount limit, so nothing capped what any single auto-approval could end up spending
memory.exp: Two layers failed: the write path stored reported speech as a user assertion, and the read path let memory function as a privileged instruction. D (amount limits) and approval gates are necessary defense-in-depth but don't fix the poisoned store; A misses that this is an architecture gap, not a model-size gap.

memory.q: Which design choice is simultaneously a trust feature AND a correctness feature for user-facing memory?
o: A cryptographic audit log proving that no memory was tampered with after it was first written to the store
User-visible, editable memory, users correct wrong facts, and transparency builds calibrated trust
Automatic expiry of every memory after 30 days, so stale facts are bounded and can't quietly outlive their truth
Admin-only memory editing, so a controlled set of operators can guarantee the integrity of what's stored
memory.exp: Visibility gives you free error correction (correctness) and consent (trust) in one feature. Audit logs (A) prove integrity of possibly-wrong data; blanket expiry (C) deletes true facts on schedule; admin-only editing (D) optimizes integrity while blocking the person who actually knows the truth.

agents.q: A process has 6 well-defined steps that never vary. The team built an autonomous agent for it. Your assessment:
o: Acceptable as long as the loop carries solid iteration caps and budget bounds to keep the runtime cost of path-choosing contained
Make it a workflow: enumerable paths get predictable, debuggable, cheap orchestration, agents are for paths you can't enumerate
Reasonable: an agent future-proofs the design for the day the six fixed steps eventually start varying and need runtime flexibility
Keep the agent but pin it with a plan-then-execute pattern so it reliably commits to following the same six steps in order every run
agents.exp: Runtime path-choosing is pure cost when the path is known: new failure modes, harder debugging, more tokens, for zero flexibility benefit. A bounds the waste without removing it; C pays today for hypothetical variance; D re-implements a workflow inside an agent, the worst of both.

agents.q: An agent with 95% per-step reliability runs a 20-step task. Expected end-to-end success, roughly:
o: ~80%, most step failures are locally recoverable and the task absorbs them without sinking
~36%, per-step error compounds multiplicatively across all 20 steps (0.95^20), with no recovery
~60%, compounding applies but built-in verification absorbs roughly half of the failures
~95%, reliability is measured per step and that same figure carries cleanly end-to-end
agents.exp: 0.95^20 ≈ 0.36. The distractors describe what people WISH were true: recovery (A) and absorption (C) only exist if you build verification gates, which is precisely why the math makes gates, fewer steps, and sharper tools the three levers that matter.

agents.q: Your agent periodically declares a half-finished task complete. The most effective fix:
o: A second reviewer agent inspects and approves the first agent's completion claims before they land
Strengthen the prompt with firm wording: 'be exhaustive; never stop before absolutely everything is done'
A harness-verified completion contract, tests or a structured checklist that code, not the model, validates
Lower the sampling temperature so the agent behaves more conservatively and stops declaring early
agents.exp: Premature victory needs external ground truth. A reviewer agent (A) is the tempting one, but it swaps one model's self-report for another model's opinion, still ungrounded; useful as a layer, not as the foundation. Prompt exhortations (B) and temperature (D) don't create verification.

agents.q: Which action class should ALWAYS carry a human approval gate in a production agent?
o: Any tool call that issues an external network request to a system outside your boundary
Any operation that reads or touches a customer's personal data in the course of the task
Irreversible or destructive operations: sends, deletes, payments, production deploys
Every state mutation the agent performs, regardless of whether the change is reversible
agents.exp: The gate criterion is irreversibility, one-way doors get humans. B is the tempting over-trigger: plenty of PII-touching reads are routine and gating them all kills the agent's usefulness (access control belongs at the tool layer). A and D gate by mechanism rather than consequence.

agents.q: The fastest path to improving a struggling production agent is usually:
o: Swap in the newest flagship model and re-run the full evaluation suite to measure the lift
Add a critic agent that reviews and signs off on each step before it is allowed to execute
Double the iteration budget so the agent has room to recover from its missteps mid-task
Sharpen the tools: clearer descriptions, instructive errors, narrower scopes, and a pruned tool list
agents.exp: Most 'agent stupidity' is tool-design debt, the model reads your descriptions every call and debugs from your error messages. Model swaps (A) ride someone else's roadmap; critics (B) add cost and latency atop the unfixed root cause; bigger budgets (C) fund more flailing.

agents.q: Your agent averages 18 steps per task at $0.02/step, running 20,000 tasks/month. A harness refactor costs $15,000 in engineering time and would cut average steps to 11. Payback period:
o: ~1.9 months
~3.2 months
~5.4 months
Never, at this step count, a better model is a higher-leverage investment
agents.exp: Baseline: 20,000 × 18 × $0.02 = $7,200/month. After refactor: 20,000 × 11 × $0.02 = $4,400/month. Monthly savings: $2,800. Payback: $15,000 ÷ $2,800 ≈ 5.4 months. A (~1.9 months) divides the refactor cost by baseline spend ($7,200) instead of savings ($2,800), it counts all spend as savings, which it isn't. B (~3.2 months) divides by post-refactor spend ($4,400) instead of savings, same error in the other direction. D is wrong on the logic: a better model doesn't change step count, which is what drives cost here. Harness investment reduces steps; model upgrades improve per-step quality. They're different levers.

agents.q: An agent tasked with researching 7 competitors spends 47 tool calls covering only 2 of them before hitting the iteration cap. The ARCHITECTURAL fix:
o: Double the iteration cap so the single agent eventually reaches coverage of all 7 competitors
Add a critic agent that monitors coverage in flight and redirects the worker after each competitor
Decompose: a planner emits 7 sub-tasks; a worker agent handles each competitor with its own tool-call budget
Expand the context window so all 7 competitors' research can be gathered within a single pass
agents.exp: Without per-unit allocation, the agent spends its full budget however it wants, and fixating on two competitors is rational local behavior with no global constraint. Decomposition makes coverage an architectural guarantee: the orchestrator can't succeed unless all 7 workers return results. Doubling the cap (A) gives the agent more money to spend unevenly; the critic (B) detects the problem late without structurally preventing it.

agents.q: Production agent logs show it sometimes calls cancel_order() before verify_payment_received(), causing incorrect cancellations. The system prompt already says 'always verify payment before cancelling.' The correct fix:
o: Strengthen the system prompt with an explicit worked example showing the correct verify-then-cancel sequence
Enforce tool availability at the harness level, cancel_order is only exposed after verify_payment_received returns success
Add a human approval gate on cancel_order so a person signs off before any cancellation executes
Switch to a reasoning model that plans the full sequence of tool calls upfront before acting on any
agents.exp: Prompt instructions compete with task pressure and fail exactly in the high-stakes cases where they matter most. Making the wrong call sequence architecturally impossible, by gating cancel_order behind a successful payment verification result, removes the failure class entirely. Human gates (C) are good defense-in-depth but the agent can still call them in the wrong order. Architectural constraints beat behavioral instructions for safety-critical sequences.

agents.q: A multi-session coding agent restarts from scratch each session, ignoring progress from prior sessions. Root cause and fix:
o: The context window is too short, so raise the max token limit and let each session simply run longer before it runs out of room
No durable state: write a structured progress artifact (files changed, approach taken, remaining work) at session end and read it back at session start
Compaction is silently deleting prior progress, so raise the compaction threshold so it fires later and keeps earlier work in the window
The agent needs a vector embedding store that persists a semantic memory of everything it did across all of the prior coding sessions
agents.exp: Each new session is amnesiac by design, the prior transcript is gone. Durable files are the proven fix: structured state the next session reads at boot, independent of context length or compaction settings. Longer sessions (A) delay the problem. Embedding stores (D) retrieve semantic content but can't restore structured progress state or track which commits were made as reliably as a file the agent wrote and can directly read.

agents.q: An agent generates 2,100 tokens of verbose reasoning narration per action turn but only 180 tokens constitute the actual action output. At 10,000 tasks/month with 6 action turns each, and output priced at $15/M tokens, what is the monthly overhead cost of the narration?
o: ~$990/month
agents.exp: Narration overhead per turn: 2,100 − 180 = 1,920 tokens. Total per month: 10,000 × 6 × 1,920 = 115.2M tokens. Cost: 115.2 × $15 = $1,728/month, closest to C (~$1,725). A uses wrong overhead (applies full 2,100 tokens as cost rather than just the 1,920-token overhead delta); B divides by a different denominator; D double-counts by applying per-turn cost to all turns rather than just overhead tokens. The fix, a structured action schema or a scratchpad field excluded from the response, eliminates this overhead entirely.

tools.q: The model keeps calling search_orders when search_invoices is correct. Fix FIRST:
o: Rewrite both descriptions with explicit use-when / don't-use-when guidance and examples
Add an intent classifier that forces tool_choice for the model before it ever sees the raw request
Merge the two into one search tool with a 'type' parameter that the model has to set on each call
Collect a corpus of selection traces and fine-tune the model on the correct tool choice for each
tools.exp: Descriptions are the model's only documentation, re-read every call, ambiguity there is the usual culprit and the five-minute fix. Forced routing (B) is legitimate but adds a component to compensate for fixable docs; merging (C) trades a selection error for a parameter error; fine-tuning (D) is weeks of work for a documentation bug.

tools.q: A tool returns 'Error 400' on bad input and the agent flails. The better design:
o: Retry the call server-side with backoff a few times before surfacing any failure back to the model
Return instructive errors, 'date must be YYYY-MM-DD, got 6/10/26', so the model can self-correct
Return an empty result set so the agent loop keeps moving past the failure instead of stalling on it
Halt the loop the moment a tool errors and escalate straight to a human to handle the bad input
tools.exp: Error text re-enters context as the model's debugging information, write it like coaching. Silent retries (A) help for transient faults but a malformed date will fail forever; empty results (C) teach the model that the data doesn't exist, which is worse than an error; halting (D) turns every recoverable mistake into an escalation.

tools.q: A tool accepts user_id as a model-supplied parameter for fetching private data. Verdict:
o: Acceptable as long as the tool is strictly read-only and every response it returns is written to an audit log
Acceptable if the server first validates that the supplied user_id exists and is well-formed before it acts on it
Privilege escalation by design: identity must come from server-side session context, never from model-generated arguments
Acceptable at temperature 0, where the model sticks to the IDs it was given and won't improvise an unauthorized one
tools.exp: B is the trap, format validation confirms the ID is real, not that the model may act for it. The model is not a principal: anything it generates is untrusted, including identities, and injection can steer it. Read-only (A) softens impact, not the violation; temperature (D) is irrelevant to trust boundaries.

tools.q: The problem MCP (Model Context Protocol) actually solves:
o: A standard authentication and authorization layer that governs how AI systems get access to tools
Tool integrations written once, usable by any compliant model or harness, ending per-app bespoke integrations
A versioned schema-negotiation handshake so different model providers can agree on tool formats
Faster structured-output decoding by letting the model use schemas registered ahead of time
tools.exp: MCP is the interop standard, the USB-C move: servers expose tools/resources once; Claude, IDEs, and other harnesses all consume them. Auth (A) and schema mechanics (C, D) are details within or adjacent to the protocol, not the problem it exists to solve.

tools.q: Answering one query requires three independent lookups; the agent runs them one per turn. The improvement:
o: Cache all three results so any later query needing the same data can skip the lookups entirely
Merge the three lookups into one composite tool, guaranteeing the whole answer takes a single round trip
Acceptable as-is, since serial execution preserves ordering and keeps the trace simpler to follow
Emit them as parallel tool calls in a single turn, independent calls batch, cutting latency ~3×
tools.exp: Modern models batch independent calls natively; serial-only loops are a silent latency tax. Caching (A) helps repeat traffic, not the first user; a composite tool (B) couples unrelated operations and bloats its own contract; 'ordering' (C) is exactly what independence means you don't need.

harness.q: Princeton HAL's CORE-Bench evaluations showed Opus 4.5 scoring ~78% under a Claude Code scaffold and 42% under the generic CORE-Agent scaffold, a 36-point gap from the same model. The defensible conclusion:
o: The benchmark itself is flawed, a result that unstable across harnesses shouldn't inform any decision
Multi-step capability is a model+harness property; scaffolding quality can outweigh model choice
The weaker harness was simply misconfigured; set up properly, that 36-point gap would mostly close
Benchmarks should mandate one reference harness so models can be compared fairly in isolation
harness.exp: Same model, 36-point spread, the scaffolding (context management, verification, recovery) IS capability on agentic work. C assumes away the finding (the 'misconfiguration' is the harness quality difference); D is a reasonable methodology wish that dodges the engineering lesson; A shoots the messenger.

harness.q: In the harness-as-operating-system analogy, context curation corresponds to:
o: The boot sequence, which initializes the system prompt and registers the session's hooks at startup, before any tool runs or work begins
Device drivers, the standardized interfaces through which the agent reaches its tools and its installed skills regardless of their backend
RAM management, deciding what's loaded in the window, what's paged out by compaction, and what's fetched on demand later
The scheduler, allocating turns across the main agent loop and the spawned sub-agents so each piece of work gets its slice of execution
harness.exp: All four mappings are real parts of the analogy, that's the point of it. Context curation specifically is memory management: loading, eviction (compaction), and demand paging (JIT retrieval). Boot = prompt/hooks setup; drivers = tool interfaces; scheduler = loop/sub-agent orchestration.

harness.q: A long-running coding agent keeps 'one-shotting', attempting the whole app, dying mid-context with undocumented state. Anthropic's proven fix:
o: A thorough planning phase that fully outlines every feature, interface, and data model before any single line of the application code is ever written down
Automatic checkpointing that snapshots the entire conversation transcript every N tool calls so the agent can roll back to any earlier point in the run
An initializer agent builds the environment (init script, JSON feature checklist, initial commit), then each session completes ONE verified feature
A much larger context window so the agent can fit a complete, multi-feature implementation inside one continuous session without ever running out of room
harness.exp: The published pattern pairs environment setup with incremental, verified, artifact-logged progress, each amnesiac session boots from durable state. Planning alone (A) still one-shots the execution; transcript checkpoints (B) preserve the mess rather than structure the work; bigger windows (D) delay the wall and worsen the crash.

harness.q: Why did Anthropic use JSON for the agent's feature checklist, with instructions to only flip a 'passes' field, instead of Markdown?
o: JSON parses reliably every single time, which lets the harness render a live progress dashboard straight from the checklist file on each run
Models are less likely to inappropriately rewrite structured JSON, and constrained edits stop the agent deleting requirements to 'pass'
JSON tokenizes far more compactly than the equivalent Markdown, shaving real context cost off of every single read of the checklist file
Git diffs on JSON stay line-stable across edits, which makes the session-over-session progress review much easier for a human to follow
harness.exp: It's a guardrail against the agent gaming its own success criteria: models treat structured JSON as less editable than prose, and the flip-one-field rule constrains the temptation. A, C, and D are all true-sounding engineering perks, none is the published reason.

harness.q: Each new session of a multi-window agent should BEGIN by:
o: Resuming precisely where the previous transcript left off, replaying its tool calls to preserve momentum across the session gap
Running the full project test suite end to end, top to bottom, before reading any of the existing project state or progress notes
Asking the orchestrator or user for an entirely fresh brief each time, to avoid inheriting any stale assumptions from the prior run
Orienting: read progress notes and git log, run the init check, verify basic state, then select ONE work item
harness.exp: Boot-sequence discipline catches yesterday's undocumented breakage before building on it. 'Resuming' (A) assumes a transcript the amnesiac session doesn't meaningfully have; full test suites (B) cost time the targeted boot-check covers; asking for a brief (C) discards the durable state that exists precisely to answer that question.

harness.q: Your team proposes hand-rolling the agent loop 'in a sprint, it's just a while loop.' The experienced counter:
o: A hand-rolled loop simply can't reach key provider features like parallel tool calls and prompt-prefix caching, so it hard-caps your performance ceiling
The loop is the easy 10%; proven harnesses embody years of compaction, permissions, resume, and verification engineering you'd rebuild badly under deadline
An in-house agent loop creates unbounded legal liability around its actions that the compliance team will eventually step in and permanently block
Provider SDKs are contractually mandated for any production tool use, so rolling your own loop is barred outright by the very terms you already agreed to
harness.exp: It IS just a while loop, for the demo. Production is the forty failure modes around it: context exhaustion, premature victory, crash recovery, permission gates. A, C, and D are false as stated; the real argument is engineering economics, same as not hand-rolling a web framework.

harness.q: A junior engineer asks why Claude Code keeps a MEMORY.md index file separate from CLAUDE.md instead of putting all memory in one file. The accurate explanation:
o: MEMORY.md is always loaded into context on every single turn, while CLAUDE.md is pulled in only when the model explicitly requests it for the task at hand
MEMORY.md is a lightweight index that lets the model triage relevance before loading full memory files; CLAUDE.md holds structural facts relevant to every session, different recall patterns

CLAUDE.md begins to measurably degrade context performance once it grows past roughly 500 lines, so any overflow memories beyond that hard line are automatically split off into a separate MEMORY.md file
MEMORY.md is synced to the cloud so the whole team shares one copy, while CLAUDE.md stays a strictly local-only file that is never allowed to leave the machine
harness.exp: The separation is a context management decision: CLAUDE.md contains facts always relevant to every session (project structure, commands, conventions). MEMORY.md is an index of selectively-loaded memories, reading its one-line descriptions lets the model decide what's relevant without loading full files into every context. This is JIT retrieval applied to agent memory.

harness.q: An agent session fails at step 23 of a 30-step plan with a tool error. The next session reads the progress artifact and resumes at step 24, but reintroduces a bug fixed in step 17. What progress artifact design flaw caused this?
o: The artifact tracked completed steps but not the decisions, constraints, and rationale that informed each step
The session crashed at step 23 before it ever managed to flush the in-progress artifact safely to disk at all
Step 24 should have automatically re-run steps 17 through 23 again as a full verification pass before it proceeded
The progress artifact should have been committed straight to git instead of being kept as a flat local working file
harness.exp: A checklist of completed steps ≠ the context of how they were completed. Step 17 fixed a bug, the fix was a decision the next session needed to inherit, but only the 'completed' flag was recorded. A robust progress artifact captures key discoveries, architectural decisions, and non-obvious constraints, not just done/not-done flags. The session at step 24 had no way to know about the step-17 constraint.

harness.q: Your harness compacts context when it reaches 80% of the 200K window. Post-compaction resets the window to 8K tokens. Each work unit generates approximately 3,000 tokens. How many work units complete between the first and second compaction events?
o: ~37 units
~50 units
~51 units
~64 units
harness.exp: After first compaction: 8K tokens. Second compaction fires at 160K (80% of 200K). Available growth: 160K − 8K = 152K. Units until compaction: 152K / 3K ≈ 50.7 → ~50 units. C (~51) results from using 5K (initial system prompt size) instead of 8K (post-compaction reset size) as the start point. Understanding this math lets you right-size work units so task boundaries align naturally with compaction events.

harness.q: A developer wants to use 'Bypass Permissions' mode during interactive development to reduce approval prompts on a large refactor. The correct guidance:
o: Yes, if those same prompts were already verified in a prior session, then re-prompting on this refactor adds no real safety value and only slows you down badly
Yes for internal tooling and one-off scripts that don't touch any user-facing surfaces or production code paths at all, where one stray action stays fully contained
Almost never during interactive work, approval prompts keep a human in the loop on unexpected tool calls; automate only in tested, scoped CI pipelines with pre-verified permissions
Yes, provided a peer reviewer will audit every single file change the refactor produces afterward, since that later review reliably catches anything the agent got wrong
harness.exp: Bypass mode is designed for automated non-interactive pipelines where the full action scope is pre-verified and no human can respond to prompts anyway. During interactive work, prompts surface unexpected behavior, the moment human oversight matters most. A large refactor touching many files is exactly when you want prompts, not when you skip them. Peer review (D) catches mistakes after the fact; prompts surface them before.

harness.q: Princeton HAL's CORE-Bench evaluations show 78% task success under a Claude Code scaffold and 42% under a generic one for the same model (Opus 4.5), a 36-point gap. Your team's agent currently scores 59% with your harness. What range is realistic from harness engineering alone?
o: Diminishing returns set in hard once you clear 50%, so harness gains realistically matter most below that line; above 59% you should expect the scaffolding to give back very little
36 points is a purely theoretical ceiling reached only under ideal lab conditions; in real day-to-day engineering practice you should expect to recover just 10 to 15 points of that lift
Potentially 75–90%, the benchmark shows harness quality can match or exceed model choice as the binding constraint; context management, verification gates, and progress artifacts are the levers
At most 5 to 10 points, since that 36-point delta was specific to Claude Code's proprietary internal infrastructure and simply won't transfer to any harness that you build yourself
